explanation.summary: Severe hypertension in pregnancy (systolic 160 or more, diastolic 110 or more) is a hypertensive emergency because of stroke and abruption risk. SOMANZ first-line is IV labetalol 20 mg over 2 minutes with dose doubling at 15 minute intervals up to 300 mg total. Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated; hydralazine is second-line at 5 mg IV, not 20 mg bolus.
key_points: Severe HTN in pregnancy: IV labetalol 20 mg then double every 15 min to 300 mg max
Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated - only oral immediate release is acceptable
Hydralazine second-line: 5 mg IV slow, not 20 mg
Pre-eclampsia with severe HTN plus end-organ signs requires simultaneous magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Sublingual nifedipine is never used in obstetric hypertensive emergency; the problem is the route, not the drug class.

options.rationale: Oral labetalol is inadequate at this BP and pace of end-organ signs (headache, epigastric pain, transaminitis, thrombocytopenia). Waiting 60 minutes on an inadequate oral dose delays control and risks stroke. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated in pregnancy for severe hypertension because of unpredictable BP drop and risk of fetal compromise. Oral nifedipine immediate release is the alternative when IV labetalol is contraindicated, but sublingual is not the route. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

Sodium nitroprusside is reserved for refractory severe hypertension and carries risk of fetal cyanide toxicity with prolonged use; it is not a first-line agent in obstetric hypertensive emergency. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

SOMANZ guideline first-line for severe hypertension in pregnancy is IV labetalol 20 mg over 2 minutes, repeated at 15 min intervals with dose doubling to a max of 300 mg. Oral labetalol has failed to control her BP so IV is appropriate. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

The SOMANZ hydralazine dose is 5 mg IV slowly, repeatable to 20 mg total; a 20 mg single bolus risks precipitous maternal hypotension and fetal bradycardia. IV labetalol is the SOMANZ first choice unless contraindicated. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria for tubal ectopic are: haemodynamic stability, bhCG under 5000 IU/L, adnexal mass under 3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, no significant pain, no haemorrhage, no MTX contraindications (normal LFT, renal, no immunodeficiency), and reliable follow up. Single-dose IM methotrexate 50 mg per m2 with day 4 and day 7 bhCG and weekly to negative is the standard.
key_points: MTX threshold for tubal ectopic is bhCG under 5000 IU/L in the RANZCOG GPS
Other MTX criteria: mass under 3.5 cm, no FCA, no significant pain, reliable follow up, normal LFT/renal
Dose is 50 mg per m2 IM as a single dose; day 4 and day 7 bhCG expected to drop 15 percent between
Surgical if unstable, ruptured, MTX contraindicated, or criteria not met
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG MTX cut-off is 5000 IU/L, not the older 3000 IU/L number.

options.rationale: Expectant management requires falling bhCG on trend; her bhCG is rising (2400 to 2900) so expectant is not indicated. Persistent or rising ectopic without treatment risks rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

This tubal ectopic meets RANZCOG methotrexate eligibility: bhCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, no significant pain, no haemorrhage, reliable follow up, normal LFTs and renal function. Single-dose IM methotrexate is the correct medical management with day 4 and day 7 bhCG check and weekly to negative. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

Surgical management is indicated for haemodynamic instability, rupture, contraindication to methotrexate, or when methotrexate criteria are not met (bhCG at or over 5000 IU/L, mass at or over 3.5 cm, fetal cardiac activity). She meets none of these; medical management is preferred and preserves the tube. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

Salpingostomy is a tube-preserving surgical option but is not indicated when medical management with methotrexate is safe and appropriate. Both surgical routes commit to operative recovery when medical management would work. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

One week of no intervention with a confirmed rising ectopic risks rupture within that window. The diagnosis is already established and she is a methotrexate candidate now. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

explanation.summary: PPH from atony is treated with mechanical measures (bimanual compression, uterine massage) plus uterotonic escalation. RANZCOG sequences oxytocin then ergometrine or carboprost then misoprostol. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension because of vasoconstriction; carboprost is the alternative. TXA and volume resuscitation run in parallel.
key_points: PPH uterotonic ladder: oxytocin, then ergometrine or carboprost, then misoprostol
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia
Carboprost is contraindicated in severe asthma but is the go-to when ergometrine cannot be used
TXA 1 g IV should be given in parallel within 3 hours - it does not replace uterotonics
explanation.pearls: The tone ladder splits on comorbidity - hypertension blocks ergometrine, asthma blocks carboprost, and the safe drug depends on which contraindication applies.

options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is given in parallel with uterotonics in PPH within 3 hours (WOMAN trial), but it does not replace the tonic. The primary problem is uterine atony and it needs a uterotonic first. TXA is an adjunct, not a substitute. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension because it causes marked vasoconstriction and BP rise. Her chronic hypertension makes this an unsafe choice; carboprost is the alternative uterotonic. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

Misoprostol is a third-line uterotonic in AU practice reserved for when parenteral agents are unavailable or exhausted; it has slower onset (30-60 min) than carboprost (10-15 min). RANZCOG puts parenteral agents ahead of misoprostol. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

She has active postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony. The RANZCOG ladder after uterine massage and oxytocin bolus is ergometrine or carboprost. Carboprost is preferred here because ergometrine is contraindicated in her chronic hypertension. Carboprost 250 mcg IM can be repeated every 15 min to a max of 2 mg. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

Magnesium sulfate is not a uterotonic - it is a smooth muscle relaxant used in pre-eclampsia and tocolysis. It would worsen atony and precipitate BP drop in the shocked patient. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

explanation.summary: Placental abruption after trauma classically presents with continuous abdominal pain, tender rigid uterus and disproportionately small external bleeding for the clinical picture (concealed haemorrhage). Fetal compromise plus maternal coagulopathy (low fibrinogen, high INR, thrombocytopenia) is a category 1 caesarean indication with major haemorrhage protocol activation.
key_points: Concealed abruption presents with pain and firm uterus but minimal external blood
Fetal bradycardia plus late decelerations plus maternal coagulopathy = category 1 caesarean
Category 1 timing target: delivery within 30 minutes of decision
MHP activation goes in parallel because DIC is already developing
explanation.pearls: In abruption, delaying for an ultrasound to exclude praevia costs the baby when the CTG has already made the call.

sources.label: RANZCOG Category of urgency for caesarean statement

options.rationale: Antenatal steroids are given up to 34+6 weeks; at 36+4 they are not indicated. More importantly, this fetus cannot wait 4 hours - it is compromised now. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

Her 20 week morphology already documented a fundal placenta, and TV ultrasound is time consuming in a category 1 situation. Ultrasound is also poorly sensitive for abruption; delaying delivery for imaging in a compromised fetus worsens outcome. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

Fetal bradycardia with late decelerations plus maternal DIC do not permit induction; there is no time and the CTG demands immediate delivery. Prostaglandin is contraindicated in this pattern. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

Magnesium neuroprotection is used before very preterm birth (under 30 weeks) and does not apply at 36+4. Observation for 30 minutes with fetal bradycardia and late decelerations delays delivery beyond the safe window. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

This is placental abruption with fetal compromise (late decelerations, bradycardia) and evolving maternal DIC (falling fibrinogen, rising INR, thrombocytopenia). RANZCOG mandates category 1 caesarean (delivery within 30 minutes) with major haemorrhage protocol activation because both mother and baby are in extremis. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

explanation.summary: Magnesium toxicity in pregnancy proceeds in a predictable sequence: loss of deep tendon reflexes then respiratory depression then cardiac arrest. She has accumulated magnesium because of oliguria (15 mL in the last hour) and rising creatinine. The specific reversal is stopping the infusion and giving IV calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes. Monitor urine output and reflexes hourly, keep magnesium infusion at 0.5-1 g per hour, and reduce dose in renal impairment.
key_points: Magnesium toxicity sequence: reflex loss, respiratory depression, arrest
Renal impairment or oliguria (under 30 mL per hour) accumulates magnesium rapidly
Antidote is calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 10 min
Reduce infusion rate to 0.5 g per hour in renal impairment or reduced urine output
explanation.pearls: The safety net for magnesium is reflexes and urine output at the bedside - a nurse's reflex check every hour catches toxicity before the respiratory rate drops.

options.rationale: Continuing magnesium in the face of overt toxicity worsens respiratory depression and risks arrest. Furosemide is not the immediate rescue; magnesium must be stopped and calcium gluconate given first. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

This is magnesium toxicity with the classical sequence of loss of deep tendon reflexes then respiratory depression. Her rising creatinine and low urine output have caused magnesium accumulation. Immediate management is to stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g IV over 10 minutes as the specific antidote. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

Reducing the infusion without stopping is inadequate for overt clinical toxicity; loss of reflexes plus respiratory rate 8 requires immediate reversal, not dose adjustment. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

Intubation is a rescue if the respiratory depression persists after magnesium is stopped and calcium given; it is not the first action when a specific antidote is available and can restore respiratory drive within minutes. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

There is no opioid in her medication list and her clinical picture (absent reflexes, weakness, respiratory depression on a magnesium infusion in AKI) is magnesium toxicity, not opioid. Naloxone would waste time. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: AFE is characterised by sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxaemia and coagulopathy occurring during labour, at ARM or delivery, or immediately postpartum. It is a clinical diagnosis; there is no bedside test. Management is supportive - airway, oxygen, resuscitative caesarean within 4 minutes of maternal arrest, MHP activation, ICU. Mortality remains high despite treatment.
key_points: AFE triad: sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxaemia, DIC
Temporal association with ARM, delivery, or immediate postpartum
Diagnosis is clinical; ROTEM will show consumptive coagulopathy but does not confirm AFE
Perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes of maternal arrest if not already delivered
explanation.pearls: The AFE fingerprint is coagulopathy with bleeding from IV sites and mucous membranes appearing within minutes - PE does not do that.

options.rationale: Oxytocin anaphylaxis is very rare and typically produces urticarial rash, bronchospasm and hypotension without immediate DIC. There is no rash description here and the bleeding pattern does not match anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2023)

Pulmonary thromboembolism causes acute hypoxia and haemodynamic collapse but does not produce simultaneous rapid-onset consumptive coagulopathy from IV and gum bleeding within minutes. The DIC-like coagulopathy is the AFE fingerprint. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic fluid embolism statement)

Eclampsia usually presents with a tonic-clonic seizure and post-ictal state, not the immediate coagulopathic bleeding pattern here. There is no BP surge history and the coagulopathy pattern does not fit eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023)

Uterine rupture in a G4P3 without a scarred uterus is possible but typically presents with abdominal pain, tenderness, loss of fetal station, and haemorrhagic shock without such rapid-onset consumptive coagulopathy. The temporal link to ARM and the mucosal oozing point elsewhere. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum haemorrhage GPS)

The triad of sudden cardiovascular collapse, hypoxaemia and consumptive coagulopathy (oozing from puncture sites and mucous membranes) at the time of ARM or delivery is classical for amniotic fluid embolism (AFE). Diagnosis is clinical; treatment is supportive with immediate resuscitative caesarean if maternal arrest, massive transfusion protocol and ICU. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic fluid embolism statement)

explanation.summary: This T14-flip scenario tests the historical-bilaterality inversion: the standard teaching that a prior contralateral salpingectomy should push you toward salpingostomy to preserve the only remaining tube is over-ruled by haemodynamic instability, rupture, mass over 3.5 cm, fetal cardiac activity and bhCG well above the MTX threshold. In this real-world constellation salpingectomy is safer, definitive, and IVF becomes her fertility route.
key_points: MTX absolute contraindications include instability, rupture, FCA, mass over 3.5 cm, bhCG at or over 5000 IU/L
Salpingostomy has 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast and 15 to 20 percent recurrent same-tube ectopic
Haemodynamic instability trumps tube-preservation logic - salpingectomy is safer
Fertility via IVF is a legitimate downstream plan when both tubes are lost
explanation.pearls: The historical-bilaterality flip usually favours preservation, but rupture with instability inverts it back to salpingectomy - safety over sentiment.

options.rationale: UAE is used for postpartum haemorrhage refractory to medical management, arteriovenous malformations, and specific fibroid indications; it is not the treatment for ruptured tubal ectopic. Definitive surgical removal is required. (Source: RANZCOG Postpartum haemorrhage guideline)

Salpingostomy is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability and in ruptured ectopic because it is technically slower, has 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast rate requiring MTX follow up, and same-tube recurrence approaches 20 percent - the very tube she is trying to preserve is now maximally damaged. IVF is her fertility pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

MTX is contraindicated in haemodynamic instability, rupture, fetal cardiac activity, mass over 3.5 cm, and bhCG at or over 5000 IU/L. She fails all five of these criteria. MTX would delay definitive surgical control of bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

She has a ruptured left tubal ectopic with shock in her only remaining tube. Although salpingostomy might otherwise be preferred to preserve the only remaining tube, the RANZCOG evidence base shows salpingostomy has a 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast rate and 15 to 20 percent recurrent same-tube ectopic rate. In a haemodynamically unstable patient with a large ruptured mass, salpingectomy is safer and definitive; future fertility can be pursued via IVF. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)
She has already ruptured and is shocked; the diagnosis is made and the operating theatre needs her now. Waiting 6 hours risks exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy GPS)

explanation.summary: This is severe pre-eclampsia with proteinuria, raised transaminases, thrombocytopenia, and neurological symptoms. SOMANZ recommends IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis at 4 g loading over 15-20 minutes followed by 2 g/hr maintenance, halved to 1 g/hr when creatinine is above 100 micromol/L because magnesium is renally cleared. Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output. IM Pritchard regimen is a historical alternative and diazepam is reserved for breakthrough seizures.
key_points: SOMANZ MgSO4: 4 g load over 15-20 min then 1-2 g/hr maintenance
Halve maintenance to 1 g/hr when creatinine >100 micromol/L
Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output for toxicity
Phenytoin and diazepam are not first-line for eclampsia seizure prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: When creatinine rises above 100 micromol/L in severe pre-eclampsia, halve the magnesium maintenance to 1 g/hr; the loading dose stays 4 g.

sources.label: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline
RANZCOG statement on eclampsia and pre-eclampsia

options.rationale: SOMANZ recommends 4 g IV loading over 15-20 min then 1 g/hr maintenance for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia, with a reduced maintenance rate (1 g/hr rather than 2 g/hr) when creatinine is above 100 micromol/L. Deep tendon reflex loss and urine output under 100 mL over 4 hours trigger withholding. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: The standard maintenance dose is 2 g/hr but this must be halved to 1 g/hr when creatinine is above 100 micromol/L to avoid toxic accumulation because magnesium is renally excreted. This patient has creatinine 128 micromol/L. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: The Pritchard IM regimen is a historical alternative used where IV pumps are unavailable. In an AU tertiary setting the IV loading-plus-infusion regimen is standard because it allows real-time titration and monitoring. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Phenytoin is inferior to magnesium sulfate for eclampsia seizure prevention (Magpie and Collaborative Eclampsia Trial) and is no longer used as first-line. Magnesium is the SOMANZ standard. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Diazepam is reserved for breakthrough seizures unresponsive to magnesium; withholding magnesium in favour of diazepam prophylaxis is inappropriate and increases eclampsia risk. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

explanation.summary: This is a primary postpartum haemorrhage with atony after oxytocin. The RANZCOG uterotonic ladder is oxytocin (bolus then infusion), then ergometrine or carboprost, then misoprostol. Ergometrine is CONTRAINDICATED in hypertension because of vasoconstriction and risk of hypertensive crisis. This patient has chronic hypertension and elevated intrapartum BP, so ergometrine (and Syntometrine which contains it) must be avoided; carboprost IM is the appropriate next-line uterotonic. Tranexamic acid should be given but is not a uterotonic.
key_points: PPH uterotonic ladder: oxytocin, then ergometrine or carboprost, then misoprostol
Ergometrine (and Syntometrine) contraindicated in hypertension
Carboprost 250 mcg IM with bronchospasm precautions is next-line when ergometrine is contraindicated
TXA should be given but is haemostatic not uterotonic
explanation.pearls: In a PPH with chronic hypertension, skip ergometrine and go straight to carboprost; watch for bronchospasm in asthmatics.

options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension because it causes profound vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis. This patient has chronic hypertension and elevated intrapartum blood pressures. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)
Syntometrine contains ergometrine which is contraindicated in hypertension; giving it here risks hypertensive crisis and cerebrovascular accident. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

Repeat IM oxytocin doses without escalation to second-line uterotonics wastes time in an ongoing PPH; RANZCOG pathway is to start an oxytocin infusion (40 units in 1 L saline over 4 hours) then move to ergometrine or carboprost. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

Misoprostol 800 mcg (rectal or sublingual) is a fallback where injectable uterotonics are unavailable and is slower in onset; carboprost is preferred when it is available. Tranexamic acid should be given but is not a uterotonic. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

After oxytocin failure and where ergometrine is contraindicated by hypertension, carboprost 250 mcg IM (Hemabate, F2-alpha prostaglandin) is the next-line uterotonic per RANZCOG PPH guidance. Bronchospasm precautions are needed. Doses may be repeated up to 8 total. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: This is severe hypertension in pregnancy (BP at least 160/110 on two readings 15 minutes apart) with likely new-onset pre-eclampsia (proteinuria). SOMANZ first-line agents for acute severe hypertension in pregnancy are oral nifedipine immediate release, IV labetalol, or IV hydralazine, all in stepped protocols. Sublingual nifedipine is avoided (risk of uncontrolled fetal distress), nitroprusside is reserved for refractory cases, and ACE inhibitors are absolutely contraindicated. Furosemide is not an antihypertensive in this setting.
key_points: SOMANZ severe HTN threshold: 160/110 on two readings 15 min apart
First-line options: oral nifedipine, IV labetalol, IV hydralazine
ACE inhibitors absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic)
Sublingual nifedipine and nitroprusside avoided
explanation.pearls: For severe HTN in pregnancy at 160/110, oral nifedipine 10 mg immediate-release is a legitimate first move when IV access is not otherwise needed; sublingual is not the same drug in a different route.

sources.label: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline
RANZCOG statement on eclampsia and pre-eclampsia

options.rationale: Nitroprusside is generally avoided in pregnancy because of cyanide accumulation risk in the fetus and requires ICU-level monitoring; it is reserved for refractory hypertensive emergency after other agents have failed. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine is not recommended in pregnancy because uncontrolled rapid drops can cause fetal distress from placental hypoperfusion. Oral nifedipine, IV labetalol, or IV hydralazine at controlled doses are the SOMANZ options. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: Furosemide is not a first-line antihypertensive in pregnancy; it may worsen intravascular depletion in pre-eclampsia (which has capillary leak) and is reserved for pulmonary oedema. It does not treat the hypertension itself. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: SOMANZ acute severe hypertension in pregnancy pathway lists oral nifedipine 10 mg immediate release (repeatable at 30 minutes to a maximum of 40 mg) as a first-line option alongside IV labetalol and IV hydralazine when BP is at least 160/110. Oral nifedipine is preferred when IV access is not needed for other reasons. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are teratogenic and cause fetal renal dysgenesis; they are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. Captopril is not appropriate at any dose antenatally. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guideline

explanation.summary: This is the T14 historical-bilaterality flip: normally salpingostomy is chosen over salpingectomy to preserve fertility, but when the contralateral tube has already been removed the affected tube is the only remaining tube. Recurrent ectopic risk in the same tube after salpingostomy is 15-30 percent, which dominates the fertility calculus. RANZCOG endorses salpingectomy plus IVF as the higher cumulative live birth pathway in this specific scenario. Methotrexate is excluded by the moderate free fluid and yolk sac features, and expectant management is excluded by the mass and pain.
key_points: T14 flip: prior contralateral salpingectomy makes salpingectomy preferred over salpingostomy
Recurrent ectopic risk in same tube after salpingostomy is 15-30 percent
Methotrexate criteria: bhCG <5000, mass <3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, no significant pain, no haemorrhage
Laparotomy reserved for haemodynamic instability
explanation.pearls: In an ectopic patient with prior contralateral salpingectomy, do NOT try to preserve the only remaining tube; take it and offer IVF, because a repeat same-tube ectopic can end that tube anyway.

options.rationale: Although salpingostomy classically preserves fertility, this patient has a prior contralateral salpingectomy meaning the left tube is her only remaining tube. Recurrent ectopic risk in the same tube is 15-30 percent, so leaving a damaged tube in place risks a further ectopic in the only remaining tube. RANZCOG accepts salpingectomy in this situation to lower recurrence risk, with IVF as the future fertility pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

This ectopic has yolk sac (though no cardiac activity) and moderate free fluid; RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate require beta-hCG under 5000 IU/L (met), mass under 3.5 cm (met), no significant pain, no haemorrhage, and no fetal cardiac activity. Moderate free fluid and worsening pain move her outside methotrexate territory. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

The T14 flip: prior contralateral salpingectomy means the affected tube is the only remaining tube. Recurrent ectopic risk in the same tube (15-30 percent) after salpingostomy dominates the fertility calculus in this scenario; salpingectomy plus IVF has a better cumulative live birth outcome than salpingostomy with a high recurrence chance. RANZCOG endorses salpingectomy in this specific scenario. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

Expectant management is only appropriate for asymptomatic patients with declining beta-hCG under 1000-2000 IU/L, minimal free fluid, and no adnexal mass. This patient has a 2.8 cm mass with yolk sac, moderate free fluid, and pain. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

Laparotomy is unnecessary in a haemodynamically stable patient with an unruptured tubal ectopic; laparoscopy has lower morbidity, shorter recovery, and comparable outcomes. Laparotomy is reserved for haemodynamic instability or extensive adhesions preventing laparoscopy. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy guideline)

explanation.summary: This is shoulder dystocia. The RANZCOG HELPERR pathway is Help (call), Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal manoeuvres including Rubin II and Woods), Remove posterior arm, and Roll patient to all-fours. After McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure has failed, delivery of the posterior arm is the next-highest-yielding internal manoeuvre. Fundal pressure is CONTRAINDICATED and Zavanelli or symphysiotomy are last resorts after internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery fail.
key_points: HELPERR sequence for shoulder dystocia
After McRoberts plus SPP: internal manoeuvres or posterior arm delivery
Fundal pressure is CONTRAINDICATED (worsens impaction, brachial plexus injury)
Zavanelli and symphysiotomy are last-resort
explanation.pearls: In shoulder dystocia after failed McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, do NOT repeat the same manoeuvre; move directly to the posterior arm which has the highest resolution rate.

options.rationale: Repeat cycles of the same manoeuvre waste time; the HELPERR pathway moves promptly to internal manoeuvres after McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure has failed. Fetal head-to-body delivery interval predicts acidosis and injury. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

Delivery of the posterior arm is the RANZCOG next step after McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure fails; it converts the bisacromial diameter to the more favourable acromio-axillary and has the highest resolution rate of the internal manoeuvres. Rubin II and Woods screw are alternative internal manoeuvres. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

Fundal pressure is CONTRAINDICATED in shoulder dystocia because it worsens impaction and increases uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury risk. It should never be used. Suprapubic pressure (Rubin I) is different. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

Symphysiotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre in Australian obstetric practice after internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery have failed; it carries significant maternal morbidity and is not the next step after McRoberts fails. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

Zavanelli is a last-resort manoeuvre after internal manoeuvres and posterior arm delivery have failed; skipping directly to it is inappropriate at this stage where internal manoeuvres have not yet been attempted. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia statement)

explanation.summary: The clinical picture (constant pain, woody uterus, dark bleeding, shock, coagulopathy, fetal bradycardia) is placental abruption with maternal and fetal compromise. RANZCOG mandates category 1 caesarean in this setting; resuscitation, MTP activation, and theatre transfer occur in parallel. GA is preferred over regional anaesthesia given the coagulopathy. Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated before excluding praevia, ultrasound has poor sensitivity for abruption, and tocolysis is contraindicated.
key_points: Abruption + maternal/fetal compromise = category 1 caesarean
GA preferred if coagulopathy (fibrinogen <2 g/L, INR >1.4)
Ultrasound misses up to 50 percent of abruptions - do not delay for imaging
Tocolysis contraindicated in abruption
explanation.pearls: A woody hard tender uterus with dark PV bleeding and fetal bradycardia is abruption until proved otherwise; go to theatre with MTP activated, do not wait for ultrasound.

options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in placental abruption because it can worsen bleeding and hide clinical deterioration. Anti-D and transfusion should be given but are supportive; the primary need is delivery. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

Digital vaginal examination in undiagnosed antepartum haemorrhage before excluding praevia risks catastrophic bleeding; ultrasound must precede a digital exam. Expectant management is inappropriate given fetal compromise and maternal shock. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

Category 1 caesarean should not be delayed for steroid or magnesium administration when there is severe abruption with fetal compromise; steroids given intraoperatively (which is common practice) do not delay delivery. Regional anaesthesia is contraindicated by the coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

This is placental abruption (constant pain, woody uterus, dark blood, maternal shock, coagulopathy) with fetal compromise (fetal HR 88 with prolonged decelerations). RANZCOG mandates category 1 caesarean when there is maternal or fetal compromise from abruption. Resuscitation and MTP activation occur in parallel with theatre transfer. GA is preferred over neuraxial when there is coagulopathy (fibrinogen 1.8, INR 1.4). (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

Ultrasound has poor sensitivity for abruption (misses up to 50 percent) and is not diagnostic; delaying delivery for imaging in the face of fetal bradycardia and maternal shock costs the baby. Clinical picture of abruption plus fetal compromise mandates immediate delivery. (Source: RANZCOG APH statement)

explanation.summary: This is a twin two now in transverse lie after vaginal delivery of a cephalic twin one, with a reassuring CTG and intact membranes in a term dichorionic diamniotic pregnancy. RANZCOG endorses internal podalic version with breech extraction as the optimal approach in an experienced unit: the accoucheur grasps a fetal foot, brings it down, and performs breech extraction only breaking membranes at the last moment. This avoids the maternal morbidity of caesarean after vaginal delivery and has better outcomes than ECV, amniotomy without version, or awaiting spontaneous descent.
key_points: Internal podalic version + breech extraction is preferred for non-cephalic second twin
Break membranes as the foot is brought through, not before, to avoid cord prolapse
ECV of second twin has lower success rates than internal manoeuvres
Delivery of twin 2 within 30 minutes of twin 1 minimises neonatal morbidity
explanation.pearls: For a transverse second twin with reassuring CTG at term, internal podalic version by an experienced accoucheur beats caesarean; keep the membranes intact until you have a foot through the cervix.

options.rationale: External cephalic version of a second twin has lower success rates than internal manoeuvres in this setting and risks umbilical cord accidents from a transverse position with intact membranes. Internal podalic version is the preferred approach in an experienced unit for non-cephalic second twin. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

Amniotomy without version in a transverse lie risks cord prolapse or arm prolapse; the fetus will not descend from a transverse position. Delaying delivery of the second twin beyond about 30 minutes also increases neonatal morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

Category 1 caesarean of the second twin after vaginal delivery of the first carries substantial maternal morbidity (combined vaginal and caesarean recovery); it is reserved for cases where internal manoeuvres are not feasible or fetal compromise supervenes. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

For a non-cephalic second twin at term in an experienced unit, internal podalic version with breech extraction (grasping a fetal foot and bringing it down before amniotomy) has better outcomes than ECV or immediate caesarean when the CTG is reassuring. This is the RANZCOG-endorsed approach when the accoucheur is experienced. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

Oxytocin augmentation for a transverse lie is not standard practice and will not correct the presentation. Amniotomy without version risks cord or arm prolapse from the transverse position. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

explanation.summary: This is amniotic fluid embolism (sudden peripartum collapse with cardiac arrest and DIC after ARM). The ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest algorithm mandates delivery within 4-5 minutes to relieve aortocaval compression and improve circulation. When vaginal delivery is imminent (fully dilated, head at station +2), assisted vaginal delivery is faster and safer than perimortem caesarean. Standard ALS (chest compressions, adrenaline 1 mg, defibrillation for shockable rhythms) and MTP activation with balanced blood products for DIC occur in parallel. Fluid alone worsens coagulopathy; thrombolysis is contraindicated with active haemorrhage.
key_points: AFE presents with sudden collapse, respiratory failure, and DIC
Delivery within 4-5 minutes of arrest improves resuscitation
Assisted vaginal delivery preferred if fully dilated and station +2 or lower
MTP with balanced blood products for the DIC; avoid crystalloid-only resuscitation
explanation.pearls: In maternal cardiac arrest with cervix fully dilated and head at station +2, an emergency ventouse or forceps beats perimortem caesarean because it delivers faster with less blood loss.

options.rationale: Perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes is standard for maternal arrest at more than 20 weeks WHEN vaginal delivery is not imminent. Here the head is at station +2 with the cervix fully dilated; a category 1 assisted vaginal delivery (rotational forceps or ventouse) achieves delivery faster than caesarean and improves both maternal and fetal outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG maternal collapse statement)

Blood products are essential and should be given but delaying delivery is worse; delivery relieves aortocaval compression and dramatically improves resuscitation chances. Blood products and delivery happen together, not sequentially. (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

Salbutamol is not part of the AFE resuscitation algorithm; the mechanism is not primarily bronchospasm but multiorgan haemodynamic collapse and DIC. Fluid without blood products in massive haemorrhage worsens dilutional coagulopathy. (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

Thrombolysis in a peripartum patient with already severe coagulopathy and active haemorrhage is catastrophic. The clinical picture is AFE (sudden collapse with DIC) not PE (which usually presents with unilateral leg findings, pleuritic pain, and different haemodynamics). (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

This is amniotic fluid embolism with cardiac arrest AND imminent vaginal delivery (station +2, fully dilated). ANZCOR maternal cardiac arrest algorithm calls for delivery within 4-5 minutes to improve maternal circulation; when vaginal delivery is imminent, assisted vaginal delivery is faster and safer than perimortem caesarean. MTP activation and standard ALS with adrenaline continue in parallel. (Source: ANZCOR/RANZCOG maternal cardiac arrest)

explanation.summary: Preterm labour before 37 weeks without a current negative GBS status is managed as GBS positive with intrapartum penicillin. The standard regimen is benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g four-hourly until delivery. A prior pregnancy swab does not carry across. In true penicillin allergy cefazolin is used for low-risk anaphylaxis and clindamycin only if the isolate is confirmed susceptible.
key_points: Preterm labour without current negative GBS swab is treated as GBS positive
Prior pregnancy GBS swab does not carry over
Regimen: benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g Q4H until delivery
Clindamycin only if penicillin allergy AND susceptible isolate
explanation.pearls: In severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis), request GBS susceptibility on any available swab before defaulting to clindamycin; up to 20 percent of AU GBS isolates are clindamycin resistant and vancomycin becomes the alternative.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.rationale: A GBS swab from a previous pregnancy does not carry over; preterm labour without a current negative GBS status is treated as GBS positive with intrapartum penicillin.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.rationale: Delivery is imminent at 4 cm and four-minutely contractions; delaying antibiotics for a PCR result risks inadequate cover and PCR has variable turnaround times.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.rationale: Broad-spectrum cover including gentamicin is used for clinical chorioamnionitis, not intrapartum GBS prophylaxis in a woman without infection features.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.rationale: AU RANZCOG guidance treats preterm labour under 37 weeks without a current negative GBS status as GBS positive; benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g four-hourly is the regimen.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

options.rationale: Clindamycin is used only when penicillin is contraindicated and only after confirming isolate susceptibility; up to 20 percent of GBS isolates in AU are resistant.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention of early-onset neonatal GBS disease

explanation.summary: In an RhD-negative pregnant woman, any potentially sensitising event including abdominal trauma requires anti-D immunoglobulin. Before 12 weeks the dose is 250 IU IM; from 12 weeks the dose is 625 IU IM. Kleihauer testing is not required before 20 weeks because a single 625 IU dose neutralises any likely feto-maternal haemorrhage volume; at or after 20 weeks Kleihauer guides additional doses.
key_points: Any sensitising event triggers anti-D regardless of visible bleeding
Under 12 weeks 250 IU; from 12 weeks 625 IU IM
Kleihauer required only at 20 weeks or later
Routine antenatal prophylaxis is 1500 IU at 28 and 34 weeks
explanation.pearls: Sensitising events include amniocentesis, external cephalic version, antepartum haemorrhage and abdominal trauma; give anti-D within 72 hours of the event but a dose given within 10 days still offers partial protection.

options.rationale: Any potentially sensitising event including abdominal trauma requires anti-D regardless of visible bleeding; feto-maternal haemorrhage may occur without external signs.
250 IU is the standard dose for sensitising events before 12 weeks; at 15 weeks the standard sensitising event dose is 625 IU, and Kleihauer is not required before 20 weeks.
Kleihauer is required at or after 20 weeks only; before 20 weeks a single standard dose reliably covers the expected feto-maternal haemorrhage volume.
1500 IU is the routine antenatal prophylactic dose given at 28 and 34 weeks; the sensitising event dose at this gestation is 625 IU, not 1500.

AU NBA advice is 625 IU IM anti-D for sensitising events from 12 weeks up to and including delivery; Kleihauer is not needed before 20 weeks as the standard dose covers likely feto-maternal haemorrhage.

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding with a transvaginal ultrasound endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm requires endometrial sampling. Outpatient hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is preferred where available, particularly in women with high pretest probability such as obesity, diabetes, or Lynch syndrome. Blind pipelle sampling is acceptable when hysteroscopy is not immediately available.
key_points: PMB with endometrial thickness > 4 mm needs tissue diagnosis
Outpatient hysteroscopy plus biopsy preferred where available
Obesity, diabetes, unopposed oestrogen and tamoxifen raise pretest probability
Do not use vaginal oestrogen before diagnosis is made
explanation.pearls: In women with Lynch syndrome, endometrial cancer risk is high and screening should include annual endometrial biopsy and TVUS from age 35, not the 4 mm threshold applied to sporadic PMB.

options.rationale: Endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm in a postmenopausal woman with bleeding requires endometrial sampling. Outpatient hysteroscopy with biopsy is the preferred AU approach when available, especially in obesity and diabetes.
The AU RANZCOG threshold to reassure without tissue is 4 mm or less; at 6 mm with risk factors of obesity and diabetes, tissue diagnosis is required for safety.
A delay of 6 weeks in a symptomatic postmenopausal woman with an above threshold endometrium is inappropriate; tissue diagnosis is needed now to exclude malignancy.
Vaginal oestrogen would not be given to a woman with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding and could worsen an occult endometrial cancer if present under the endometrium.
MRI is not first line; it is used for staging once endometrial malignancy has been histologically confirmed, not for the initial diagnostic decision in postmenopausal bleeding.

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura is a UKMEC category 4 contraindication to any oestrogen-containing contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk; this includes combined oral pill, patch and vaginal ring at any dose. Progestogen-only methods are safe. The levonorgestrel intrauterine device is UKMEC category 1, highly effective and long-acting, and is the preferred option here. DMPA is acceptable but has other drawbacks compared with an IUD.
key_points: Migraine with aura: UKMEC 4 for any oestrogen-containing method
LNG-IUD is UKMEC 1 and preferred LARC in aura
Progestogen-only pill and DMPA are UKMEC 2
Route of oestrogen (oral, patch, ring) does not change the category
explanation.pearls: Aura features that trigger UKMEC 4 include any focal neurological symptom lasting under 60 minutes (visual, sensory, dysphasia); a nonspecific prodrome or postdrome without focal neurology is not aura.

options.rationale: Migraine with aura is a UKMEC category 4 contraindication to combined hormonal contraception at any dose due to ischaemic stroke risk associated with oestrogen exposure.
Progestogen-only intrauterine contraception is UKMEC category 1 in migraine with aura; it is highly effective, long-acting, reversible and does not carry the oestrogen-related ischaemic stroke risk.
Any oestrogen-containing method is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura, regardless of the route of oestrogen administration used or the specific progestogen combined with it.
DMPA is UKMEC category 2 in migraine with aura and is a reasonable option, but is not as long-acting or as low-risk for bone loss and weight gain as a LNG-IUD.
The vaginal ring contains oestrogen and remains UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura; the route does not change the ischaemic stroke risk assessment for combined hormonal methods.

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum is delivered by planned caesarean between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids, in a tertiary centre with an MDT including obstetric anaesthesia, urology, interventional radiology and blood bank. Cross-match at least 4 to 6 units of red cells. The placenta is left in situ during hysterectomy; attempted removal causes catastrophic haemorrhage.
key_points: Planned delivery 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after antenatal steroids
Do not attempt to remove the placenta at CS
MDT: MFM, anaesthesia, urology, IR, blood bank
Cross-match 4 to 6 units red cells minimum
explanation.pearls: For women declining hysterectomy who wish to preserve fertility, a Triple-P procedure or leaving the placenta in situ with methotrexate is an option, but with substantial infection and delayed bleeding risk.

options.rationale: For placenta accreta spectrum, planned delivery is 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after antenatal steroids, not 39 weeks; delay to 39 weeks risks unscheduled bleeding and emergency surgery.
Vaginal delivery is contraindicated with placenta praevia and accreta due to unmanageable haemorrhage risk; expectant management to term is unsafe in placenta accreta spectrum.
AU MFM guidance advises delivery between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks after antenatal steroids, with an MDT including anaesthesia, urology, IR and blood bank; the placenta is left in situ during hysterectomy.
Attempted manual removal in placenta accreta causes catastrophic haemorrhage; the placenta must be left in situ during hysterectomy or conservative management is chosen.
Delayed hysterectomy at 6 weeks is a conservative alternative in selected fertility-preserving cases; a Rusch balloon does not have a role and planned caesarean hysterectomy is standard.

explanation.summary: Confirmed vasa praevia requires planned inpatient admission around 32 weeks with a course of antenatal corticosteroids completed before 34 weeks. Elective caesarean is performed at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks before spontaneous rupture of membranes can cause fetal exsanguination. Outpatient management to term risks membrane rupture in transit and is not standard AU practice. Immediate delivery at 32 weeks unnecessarily commits the neonate to preterm complications when planned delivery a few weeks later is safer.
key_points: Confirmed vasa praevia: admit around 32 weeks, steroids, deliver 34 to 36 weeks
Vaginal delivery contraindicated
Outpatient management to term is not standard
Emergency caesarean if any ROM or bleeding regardless of gestation
explanation.pearls: A 50 mL fetal bleed can exsanguinate a term fetus; do not wait for an abnormal CTG. If membranes rupture with bleeding, category 1 caesarean is warranted for suspected vasa praevia bleeding.

options.rationale: 39 weeks is too late; the risk of membrane rupture and fetal exsanguination rises after 34 weeks. Inpatient admission and steroids are usually recommended from around 32 weeks.
Waiting to 39 weeks after admission and steroids exposes the pregnancy to spontaneous rupture and fetal exsanguination; planned delivery is at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after steroids.
Outpatient management to 37 weeks exposes the pregnancy to risk of membrane rupture during transit; inpatient admission and earlier planned delivery are preferred.

AU RANZCOG supports inpatient admission around 32 weeks, antenatal steroids completing before 34 weeks, and elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks before spontaneous rupture and haemorrhage can occur.
Immediate delivery at 32 weeks exposes the neonate to unnecessary preterm complications; the risk-benefit balance favours planned delivery at 34 to 36 weeks after steroids.

explanation.summary: Severe OHSS with tense ascites, oliguria, haemoconcentration (haematocrit above 0.45) and pleural effusion requires hospital admission. Manage with cautious IV crystalloid or colloid to restore intravascular volume, human albumin as oncotic support, prophylactic-dose enoxaparin (severe OHSS is a strong VTE risk), and ultrasound-guided paracentesis for symptomatic ascites or effusion. Diuretics and fluid restriction are contraindicated as they worsen haemoconcentration and thrombosis.
key_points: Severe OHSS: admit, cautious IV fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Paracentesis for symptomatic tense ascites or effusion
Diuretics contraindicated in third-space phase
Cabergoline is a preventive measure, not a treatment at this stage
explanation.pearls: Cabergoline 0.5 mg daily started on the day of hCG trigger for 8 days reduces the incidence of moderate-to-severe OHSS by modulating VEGF-mediated vascular permeability.

options.rationale: Cabergoline is a preventative pre-trigger measure; this severe hospital-requiring presentation cannot be safely managed as an outpatient with oral therapy and follow-up.
Furosemide worsens intravascular depletion and haemoconcentration in OHSS; loop diuretics are contraindicated in the third-space phase of the illness where extravascular fluid predominates.
Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin is standard for severe OHSS; therapeutic dose is reserved for confirmed VTE and CT-PA is only warranted if suspicion is high, not from ascites-related dyspnoea alone.
Fluid restriction and diuretics worsen haemoconcentration and thrombotic risk in severe OHSS; outpatient care is inappropriate with haematocrit above 0.45 plus oliguria and tense ascites.
Severe OHSS with tense ascites, oliguria, haemoconcentration and effusion requires admission with careful crystalloid or colloid, VTE prophylaxis and paracentesis for symptomatic relief.

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome from postpartum haemorrhage causes panhypopituitarism with hypocortisolism, hypothyroidism and central diabetes insipidus in some patients. The immediate priority is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV every 6 hours to prevent adrenal crisis, correction of hypoglycaemia with dextrose, and cautious hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia. Thyroxine must be started after glucocorticoid replacement because unopposed thyroxine can precipitate adrenal crisis.
key_points: Hydrocortisone before thyroxine in panhypopituitarism
Dextrose for hypoglycaemia, cautious hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia
Fludrocortisone not required in secondary adrenal insufficiency
Synacthen test and other confirmatory tests come after treatment
explanation.pearls: The classical Sheehan triad of failure to lactate, secondary amenorrhoea and postural symptoms may not appear until months after the causative haemorrhage; a low index of suspicion for hypopituitarism in postpartum fatigue and hyponatraemia is warranted.

sources.label: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.rationale: In panhypopituitarism, glucocorticoid replacement must precede thyroxine to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis, along with dextrose for hypoglycaemia and cautious hypertonic saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.rationale: Thyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement in panhypopituitarism can precipitate adrenal crisis by increasing metabolic demand on unreplaced cortisol; steroids must be given first.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.rationale: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia needs dextrose and severe symptomatic hyponatraemia at 122 warrants cautious hypertonic saline; deferring thyroxine indefinitely once cortisol is replaced is inappropriate.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not required in secondary adrenal insufficiency since aldosterone secretion is preserved via the RAAS; hydrocortisone is the correct first agent for the cortisol deficit.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

options.rationale: Delaying life-saving replacement to complete a synacthen test in a haemodynamically unstable postpartum woman is inappropriate; treat first and confirm the diagnosis later.
source_refs: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hypopituitarism

explanation.summary: Australian ADIPS criteria diagnose gestational diabetes on the 75 g OGTT if any one value meets: fasting >=5.1, 1 hour >=10.0 or 2 hour >=8.5 mmol/L. One abnormal value is sufficient. Initial management is structured education, self-monitoring of capillary glucose four times daily (fasting plus 2 hours post each main meal) and dietitian review, with metformin or insulin added within 1 to 2 weeks if targets are not met.
key_points: One value at or above ADIPS threshold diagnoses GDM in AU
Fasting 5.1, 1 hr 10.0, 2 hr 8.5 mmol/L are the cut-offs
Lifestyle plus glucose monitoring for 1 to 2 weeks first-line
Add metformin or insulin if targets not met on lifestyle
explanation.pearls: Postpartum 75 g OGTT at 6 to 12 weeks is mandatory as approximately 50 percent of women with GDM develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years; women should be counselled about this trajectory at diagnosis to reinforce postpartum follow-up.

options.rationale: AU ADIPS criteria require only one abnormal value, and her fasting glucose meets the threshold; repeating in 4 weeks delays management and increases fetal risk from ongoing hyperglycaemia.
AU ADIPS criteria diagnose GDM on any of fasting >=5.1, 1 hr >=10.0 or 2 hr >=8.5; her fasting of 5.4 exceeds the threshold so she meets diagnostic criteria and enters the standard care pathway.
AU pathway is lifestyle first for 1 to 2 weeks with glucose monitoring, adding metformin or insulin only if glycaemic targets are not met; jumping to metformin skips the standard trial period.
Overt diabetes in pregnancy is defined by fasting glucose >=7.0, random >=11.1 or HbA1c >=6.5; her values do not meet the overt diabetes cut-offs so GDM management is appropriate.
Deferring diagnosis to 34 weeks misses 6 to 8 weeks of glycaemic control and increases the risk of macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and neonatal hypoglycaemia.

explanation.summary: External cephalic version should be offered to all women with a singleton breech presentation at 37 weeks in the absence of contraindications (praevia, uterine scar in some settings, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy, fetal compromise, coagulopathy, antepartum haemorrhage). Success is approximately 50 percent and reduces caesarean rate. The procedure requires tocolysis with terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneously, CTG monitoring before and after and access to caesarean facilities.
key_points: Offer ECV at 37 weeks in eligible women with breech
Success rate approximately 50 percent
Terbutaline 250 microgram SC tocolysis; CTG before and after
Must have immediate caesarean facilities available
explanation.pearls: In RhD-negative women, anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU IM is given after ECV regardless of outcome because ECV is a sensitising event; Kleihauer is performed if at 20 weeks or beyond to guide any additional dosing.

options.rationale: ECV has approximately 50 percent success in AU cohorts and is offered routinely; skipping ECV without offer is not consistent with RANZCOG guidance and denies informed choice.
ECV timing is 37 weeks to allow spontaneous version, and salbutamol IV is not the AU tocolytic of choice; terbutaline SC is standard for ECV.
Vaginal breech birth is possible in selected women but ECV should be offered first as it converts to cephalic and lowers overall caesarean rate; jumping to VBB skips the safer first step.

AU RANZCOG guidance recommends ECV from 37 weeks in eligible women with tocolysis, CTG monitoring before and after, and immediate caesarean facilities; there are no contraindications in this scenario.
Moxibustion evidence is weak and best used before 34 weeks; at 36+5 the priority is offering ECV at 37 weeks which has a stronger evidence base and is the AU-recommended intervention.

explanation.summary: For atonic primary PPH after prophylactic oxytocin, the AU next-line uterotonic is ergometrine 250 microgram IV slow bolus with tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of onset. Carboprost 250 microgram IM is added if bleeding continues (contraindicated in asthma). Concurrent measures include bimanual uterine compression, bladder emptying, warmed IV crystalloid, group and crossmatch and senior obstetric review. Failed medical measures escalate to Bakri balloon then surgical control.
key_points: Ergometrine + TXA is next-line after prophylactic oxytocin
TXA reduces mortality if given within 3 hours (WOMAN trial)
Bimanual compression while pharmacological measures work
Bakri balloon after failed medical management before surgery
explanation.pearls: Ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, cardiac disease and Raynaud phenomenon; in these women carboprost is preferred if not asthmatic, or misoprostol 800 microgram sublingually is an alternative uterotonic.

sources.label: WOMAN trial and AU PPH pathway

options.rationale: In a soft high uterus with ongoing atonic PPH after prophylactic oxytocin, next-line uterotonic is ergometrine plus IV TXA 1 g; bimanual compression, resuscitation and senior review complete the initial bundle.
source_refs: WOMAN trial and AU PPH pathway

options.rationale: Magnesium is uterine relaxant and worsens atony; carboprost is a valid uterotonic but not the AU next-line before ergometrine plus TXA in an unallergic non-hypertensive woman.
A second oxytocin dose after prophylactic oxytocin is not first-line escalation; the next-line uterotonic is ergometrine and adding TXA within 3 hours of onset lowers mortality.
Bakri balloon is appropriate after failed medical management; skipping the pharmacological escalation is not the AU recommended stepwise approach when brief medical measures have not been attempted.
There is no indication for empirical vitamin K or FFP before coagulation results; the priority is uterotonic escalation with ergometrine plus TXA and mechanical measures.

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome with severe features (BP >=160/110, headache, visual disturbance, hyperreflexia, RUQ pain, evidence of end-organ damage) at 33+2 weeks requires IV magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/hour infusion for eclampsia prophylaxis, tight BP control with labetalol or hydralazine to <150/100, betamethasone for fetal lung maturity and delivery within 24 to 48 hours. Dexamethasone does not improve maternal outcomes. Mode of delivery is by obstetric indication.
key_points: HELLP with severe features triggers MgSO4 loading and BP control
Betamethasone before 34 weeks
Deliver within 24 to 48 hours; do not delay to term
Dexamethasone does not improve maternal HELLP outcomes
explanation.pearls: Watch for subcapsular liver haematoma when RUQ pain worsens with falling haemoglobin and platelet drop; urgent CT or MRI abdomen and multidisciplinary review with hepatobiliary surgery are essential, and hepatic rupture carries maternal mortality above 50 percent.

options.rationale: Expectant management to 37 weeks in HELLP with severe features is not recommended; delivery within 24 to 48 hours after steroids is the AU standard given ongoing maternal risk of stroke, DIC and eclampsia.
Plasma exchange is not first-line for HELLP unless progression to thrombotic microangiopathy is confirmed; magnesium is mandatory for eclampsia prophylaxis in severe features.

This is HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) with severe features (BP >=160/110, visual disturbance, brisk reflexes); magnesium seizure prophylaxis, BP control and expedited delivery after steroid loading are AU standard.

Fetal status is reassuring and betamethasone significantly reduces neonatal morbidity at 33 weeks; skipping magnesium raises eclampsia risk and furosemide is not the AU first-line antihypertensive here.
Dexamethasone does not modify maternal outcome in HELLP; the definitive treatment is delivery, expedited within 24 to 48 hours after antenatal betamethasone at 33 weeks.

explanation.summary: Chorioamnionitis complicating PPROM is diagnosed by maternal fever plus one or more of maternal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia, or purulent discharge with supporting rising inflammatory markers. Management is IV ampicillin plus gentamicin (metronidazole added intrapartum or postpartum for anaerobic cover), expedited delivery regardless of gestation and neonatal team notification. Tocolysis and expectant care are contraindicated once chorioamnionitis is suspected.
key_points: Fever + uterine tenderness + fetal tachycardia = chorioamnionitis
IV ampicillin + gentamicin (add metronidazole intrapartum) is AU standard
Deliver expeditiously regardless of gestation
Tocolysis contraindicated once chorioamnionitis suspected
explanation.pearls: Latency erythromycin (per ORACLE I) prolongs pregnancy in PPROM without chorioamnionitis; amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is avoided due to increased necrotising enterocolitis risk (per ORACLE II) despite being effective for maternal outcomes.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Once chorioamnionitis is clinically suspected, latency antibiotics are no longer appropriate; continued expectant care risks maternal sepsis and neonatal early-onset sepsis.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Antipyresis and observation delay definitive treatment; chorioamnionitis is a maternal and fetal emergency requiring IV antibiotics and delivery, not oral macrolide alone.

Chorioamnionitis needs anaerobic and Gram-negative cover which ceftriaxone monotherapy does not reliably provide; standard AU regimen is ampicillin plus gentamicin (add metronidazole intrapartum or postpartum).
Tocolysis is contraindicated when chorioamnionitis is present as it may worsen maternal sepsis and delay life-saving delivery.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Maternal fever, tachycardia, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia and rising inflammatory markers on PPROM meet AU chorioamnionitis criteria; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and expedited delivery are indicated regardless of gestation.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion classically presents as sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with an enlarged tender adnexa and absent Doppler flow on transvaginal ultrasound. Any woman with these features requires emergency laparoscopy for detorsion. Contemporary AU practice favours ovarian preservation with cystectomy even for dusky-appearing ovaries, as most regain function; oophorectomy is reserved for confirmed necrosis or suspicion of malignancy.
key_points: Sudden pain + enlarged ovary + absent Doppler flow = torsion
Emergency laparoscopy is the standard next step
Detorsion preserves function even in dusky ovaries
Oophorectomy reserved for confirmed necrosis or malignancy
explanation.pearls: Ovarian torsion risk is highest with ovarian masses between 5 and 10 cm (very large masses are anchored, very small ones do not create torque); the underlying cyst should be removed after detorsion, ideally at the same procedure to reduce recurrence risk.

options.rationale: PID typically has fever, cervical motion tenderness, discharge and does not cause absent Doppler flow; treating as PID delays surgical detorsion and risks ovarian necrosis.

The sudden severe pain, palpable enlarged ovary and absent Doppler flow on TVS are diagnostic of ovarian torsion; AU consensus favours detorsion and cystectomy even for dusky ovaries because most recover function.
TVS has already shown absent Doppler flow in an enlarged ovary; CT delays definitive detorsion and adds radiation without changing the surgical indication.
Delayed detorsion risks irreversible ovarian necrosis; even suspected torsion warrants urgent surgical exploration in AU pathways.
Contemporary evidence shows dusky ovaries frequently recover function after detorsion; oophorectomy is now reserved for confirmed necrosis or malignancy on frozen section.

explanation.summary: Acute uterine inversion is a rare obstetric emergency presenting as sudden shock after delivery with an absent uterine fundus and a mass at the introitus. Immediate management is manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) with the placenta still attached, before uterotonics or attempted placental separation which cause further bleeding or make replacement impossible. Tocolysis with terbutaline may be needed if a cervical ring has formed. Uterotonics are given only after successful replacement.
key_points: Sudden shock after delivery with absent fundus = uterine inversion
Replace immediately with placenta still attached (Johnson manoeuvre)
Hold uterotonics until after successful replacement
Tocolysis with terbutaline if cervical ring prevents replacement
explanation.pearls: If manual replacement fails, escalate to O'Sullivan hydrostatic replacement (warm saline via douche in the vagina with the vulva sealed by an assistant); operative approaches (Huntington traction on round ligaments, Haultain posterior cervical incision) are last resorts requiring laparotomy under general anaesthesia.

options.rationale: Uterotonics BEFORE replacement fix the inverted uterus in position by contracting the cervical ring; they are held until after successful replacement, then given to prevent recurrence.
Placental separation before replacement causes catastrophic bleeding; replace uterus with placenta attached first, then manage placenta after successful replacement.
Vaginal packing does not treat inversion; surgical replacement (Huntington or Haultain) is reserved for failed manual replacement, not first-line.

Acute uterine inversion is a life-threatening emergency where the AU first-line manoeuvre is immediate manual replacement (Johnson) with the placenta in situ; delay allows a cervical ring to contract and makes replacement harder.
Volume resuscitation is done concurrently, not sequentially before intervention; delay of 15 minutes worsens outcome. Replace uterus while resuscitating.

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism presents peri-delivery with sudden hypoxia, cardiovascular collapse, altered consciousness and consumptive coagulopathy. Management is simultaneous ABC resuscitation with airway control by RSI, high-flow oxygen, vasopressor support, massive haemorrhage protocol for the coagulopathy and immediate expedited delivery (perimortem caesarean within 5 minutes if cardiac arrest). Empirical treatment based on classical triad; do not delay for confirmatory imaging.
key_points: Sudden hypoxia + collapse + coagulopathy peri-delivery = AFE
Secure airway (RSI), oxygen, vasopressors, MHP
Deliver immediately (perimortem caesarean within 5 minutes if arrested)
Do not delay for CT or heparin
explanation.pearls: Contemporary management includes early use of the A-OK bundle (atropine, ondansetron, ketorolac) which targets vagal, serotonin and thromboxane pathways implicated in AFE; discuss with a maternal-critical-care team early as ECMO may be considered in refractory cases.

options.rationale: This is classical amniotic fluid embolism (sudden hypoxia, hypotension, altered conscious state and coagulopathy peri-delivery); management is airway, oxygenation, vasopressor circulatory support and immediate delivery within 5 minutes to improve maternal and fetal outcome.
AFE typically causes consumptive coagulopathy with severe bleeding; heparin worsens haemorrhage and CT scan delay is fatal. Empirical treatment based on the classical triad is standard.
There is no hypertension, and the sudden hypoxia, RV dilatation on echo and coagulopathy fit AFE; magnesium is not the treatment and delays airway and circulatory rescue.
Regional anaesthesia is contraindicated in shocked coagulopathic patient; airway must be secured with RSI and delivery expedited within minutes.

Perimortem caesarean is done after 4 minutes of arrest if ROSC not achieved, alongside continuous resuscitation; skipping airway and circulatory support in a shocked but not yet arrested woman is inappropriate.

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis made on acute onset of skin or mucosal change with either respiratory compromise or hypotension, and intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh is the first treatment in every setting, given before antihistamines, corticosteroids or fluids. In labour the picture is complicated because maternal hypotension produces a prolonged fetal deceleration, and the temptation is to treat the cardiotocograph rather than the mother. Resuscitating the mother, with left lateral tilt or manual uterine displacement to relieve aortocaval compression, is what restores placental perfusion; birth is expedited only if the fetal heart fails to recover. Once she is stable, prophylaxis continues with a non beta-lactam agent, and the reaction is documented as a severe immediate penicillin allergy in her record. In context, penicillins are among the commonest triggers of drug anaphylaxis in Australian hospitals, and delay in giving adrenaline is the factor most consistently associated with poor outcome.
key_points: Anaphylaxis is skin or mucosal change plus respiratory compromise or hypotension.
Intramuscular adrenaline into the lateral thigh comes before all other drugs.
Maternal resuscitation with uterine displacement restores the fetal heart rate.
Document a severe immediate penicillin allergy and switch to a non beta-lactam.
explanation.pearls: A prolonged fetal deceleration during a maternal collapse is usually a consequence of maternal hypotension; resuscitate the mother first and the trace commonly recovers without the need for immediate birth.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines - Acute management of anaphylaxis
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis
RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

options.rationale: Hypotension and bronchospasm with weals during an infusion is anaphylaxis, and intramuscular adrenaline is the first drug in every case. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines - Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines - Acute management of anaphylaxis
Australian Medicines Handbook - benzylpenicillin and vancomycin

options.rationale: These are adjuncts for symptom relief and are reasonable once adrenaline has been given, or for isolated urticaria. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines - Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines - Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Fluid and senior help follow immediately, but giving them before adrenaline delays the only treatment that reverses the reaction. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines - Acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines - Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Choosing the replacement antibiotic matters later, once she is stable and still needs cover in labour. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - group B streptococcal prophylaxis
Australian Medicines Handbook - benzylpenicillin and vancomycin

options.rationale: Birth is expedited if the fetal heart does not recover after the mother has been resuscitated. (Source: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

explanation.summary: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate is appropriate for a haemodynamically stable woman with a tubal ectopic pregnancy meeting RANZCOG criteria: bhCG less than 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, mass smaller than 3.5 cm, minimal pain, reliable follow-up, and no contraindications. Success rates approximate 85 to 90% with these thresholds. Failure of bhCG to fall by 15% between day 4 and day 7 triggers a second dose or surgical intervention.
key_points: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria: bhCG <5000, no cardiac activity, mass <3.5 cm, minimal pain, reliable follow-up, no CI
Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM with day 4 and day 7 bhCG (>=15% fall required)
Surgical management mandated at bhCG >=5000 IU/L or cardiac activity or mass >=3.5 cm or instability
Contraindications include cytopenias, abnormal LFTs, creatinine >120, breastfeeding, hepatic or renal disease
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG surgical threshold for tubal ectopic is bhCG >=5000 IU/L (not 3000). Methotrexate remains an option below 5000 with all other criteria met.

options.rationale: Expectant management is confined to a small subset with bhCG less than 1000 IU/L, a decreasing trend, no adnexal mass or cardiac activity, and no pain. This woman has a rising bhCG above 4800 IU/L with an adnexal mass and pain, so expectant management fails RANZCOG criteria. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

The RANZCOG threshold requiring surgical management is bhCG 5000 IU/L or higher, or the presence of cardiac activity, mass 3.5 cm or larger, significant pain, haemodynamic instability, or unreliable follow-up. This woman meets none of the mandatory surgical triggers. Salpingectomy is also more invasive than methotrexate when the tube-sparing medical option remains available. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

Salpingostomy has higher rates of persistent trophoblast and is largely reserved for cases where the contralateral tube is absent or diseased. Neither medical nor surgical thresholds mandate this approach for the current presentation. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

Mifepristone-misoprostol is a medical termination regimen for intrauterine pregnancy and does not treat tubal ectopic. Trophoblast in the tube will continue to grow and risk rupture. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

This woman meets Australian RANZCOG criteria for medical management with single-dose methotrexate: bhCG below 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, mass smaller than 3.5 cm, no significant pain, haemodynamically stable, reliable for follow-up, no contraindications with normal baseline haematology, renal and liver function. Single-dose 50 mg per m2 IM is standard with day 4 and day 7 bhCG (expect >=15% fall from day 4 to day 7) and weekly bhCG thereafter. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause with failure of non-hormonal therapy is treated with low-dose vaginal estrogen. Australian AMS guidance supports this option in ER-negative breast cancer survivors with oncology agreement. Systemic HRT is disproportionate for local symptoms and ospemifene is not first-line in Australia.
key_points: Non-hormonal moisturiser and lubricant trial is first-line for GSM
Vaginal estradiol 10 mcg tablet or estriol 0.03 mg pessary, daily loading then twice-weekly maintenance
Local estrogen is acceptable in most breast cancer survivors after oncology discussion
Vaginal laser therapy is not endorsed as first-line by AMS or TGA
explanation.pearls: Systemic absorption from low-dose vaginal estradiol tablets rarely exceeds baseline postmenopausal serum estradiol; onc consent still documented case-by-case.

options.rationale: Low-dose vaginal estrogens (estradiol 10 microgram tablets or estriol 0.03 mg pessaries) produce local mucosal restoration with minimal systemic absorption and are supported by the AMS and RANZCOG for genitourinary syndrome of menopause. Recent evidence and IMS 2016 statement support use in ER-negative breast cancer survivors with oncology agreement after non-hormonal therapies fail. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society Vulvovaginal atrophy)

Systemic hormone therapy is inappropriate for isolated genitourinary symptoms and carries risks even in ER-negative disease that are hard to justify when a low-dose local option addresses the symptom directly. (Source: AMS: Vulvovaginal atrophy)

Ospemifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator not routinely available on the PBS in Australia and generally avoided in women with prior breast cancer because of uncertain breast safety. AMS advises against SERM use in breast cancer survivors. (Source: AMS: Vulvovaginal atrophy)

Vaginal laser therapy is not first-line and lacks the evidence base for efficacy and safety endorsed by the AMS and TGA; the TGA issued a safety alert in 2018. Reserve for after trial of local estrogen with oncology input. (Source: AMS: Vulvovaginal atrophy)

Post-coital spotting from a friable atrophic vagina with a normal cervix does not itself mandate hysteroscopy; if postmenopausal bleeding is truly unexplained after treatment of atrophy or if endometrium is thickened on ultrasound (>4 mm), then endometrial assessment is warranted. Directly biopsying without addressing the atrophic cause first is not the initial step. (Source: RANZCOG PMB)

explanation.summary: PPROM between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks without infection or fetal compromise is managed expectantly to prolong pregnancy with antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity and prophylactic erythromycin for 10 days to reduce infection and delay delivery. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is avoided because of increased neonatal necrotising enterocolitis risk (ORACLE I). Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is given empirically when GBS status is unknown at delivery. Delivery is planned by 37+0 weeks.
key_points: PPROM 24-33+6 weeks without infection: expectant management with steroids + 10 day erythromycin
Corticosteroids: betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 h apart (or dexamethasone 6 mg IM x4 12 h apart)
