Amoxicillin-clavulanate contraindicated in PPROM (NEC signal in ORACLE I)
Deliver by 37+0 to balance prematurity vs infection risk
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is loaded 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion when delivery is anticipated within 24 hours at <30-32 weeks gestation.

options.rationale: RANZCOG guidance for PPROM between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks without infection or fetal compromise is expectant management to prolong pregnancy, with corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x2) for fetal lung maturity, erythromycin (avoid amoxicillin with clavulanic acid in this indication because of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis signal in ORACLE I) for 10 days to prolong latency, and intrapartum GBS prophylaxis given unknown GBS status. Aim for delivery by 37+0 weeks to balance prematurity and infection risk. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

Delivery is triggered by infection, fetal compromise, placental abruption, or reaching 37 weeks. In its absence, expectant management until 37 weeks improves neonatal outcomes because prematurity below 34 weeks poses more risk than the current infectious threat. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

Discharge home is not recommended for PPROM before 34 weeks because of the risk of rapid deterioration from chorioamnionitis, abruption or cord accident. Inpatient care with regular CTG and infection surveillance is preferred. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and induction are used when chorioamnionitis is diagnosed. In their absence at 32 weeks, expectant management is preferred to allow further fetal lung maturation. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection when delivery is anticipated within 24 hours and gestation is less than 30 to 32 weeks; at 32+1 with no evidence of imminent delivery it is not routinely given. Steroids should not be deferred; they are given at diagnosis of PPROM 24 to 34 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

explanation.summary: Trial of labour after caesarean is contraindicated when the prior incision was classical (vertical upper-segment), T-incision, or inverted-T because of a substantially higher uterine rupture risk (10 to 12% vs <1% for a single low-transverse scar). RANZCOG recommends elective repeat caesarean at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks. Prostaglandin cervical ripening and oxytocin augmentation are contraindicated in prior classical caesarean pregnancies planned for delivery.
key_points: Prior classical (vertical upper-segment) CS = absolute contraindication to trial of labour
Rupture risk classical incision 10-12% vs low-transverse <1%
Elective repeat CS at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks after prior classical incision
Prostaglandin cervical ripening contraindicated after any prior CS scar (RANZCOG)
explanation.pearls: Other absolute contraindications to VBAC: prior uterine rupture, T-shaped or inverted-T scar, transverse lie or breech in labour, placenta praevia or accreta.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top 45 Birth After Caesarean Birth

options.rationale: Trial of labour is contraindicated when the prior caesarean incision was classical (vertical upper-segment) because rupture risk approaches 10 to 12% versus <1% for low-transverse. RANZCOG advises against labour in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

A prior classical (vertical upper-segment) caesarean is an absolute contraindication to trial of labour because uterine rupture rate is 10 to 12% versus under 1% for a single low-transverse incision. RANZCOG recommends elective repeat caesarean at 37+0 to 38+0 weeks to reduce the risk of labour onset while balancing neonatal maturation. Shared decision-making is documented but the recommendation should be specific. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

Elective delivery before 37+0 without a specific indication increases neonatal respiratory morbidity. Timing of elective repeat caesarean after classical incision is typically 37+0 to 38+0 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

Prostaglandin cervical ripening is contraindicated after prior classical caesarean because of markedly increased rupture risk. Expectant management to 40 weeks is inappropriate given rising labour probability. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

The baby is already cephalic, and oxytocin augmentation in a prior classical caesarean is contraindicated. External cephalic version has no role for a cephalic-presenting fetus. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

explanation.summary: Suspected placental abruption near term with active bleeding, uterine tenderness and any fetal compromise mandates urgent delivery, usually by category 1 caesarean unless vaginal delivery is imminent. Two large-bore IVs, cross-match, coagulation studies, and readiness to activate the massive transfusion protocol are simultaneous. Fibrinogen is a sensitive marker of consumption and DIC risk. Neonatal team must be present.
key_points: Placental abruption at term with maternal or fetal compromise = urgent delivery, usually category 1 CS
Two large-bore IVs, cross-match 4 units, group + coagulation profile including fibrinogen
Fibrinogen <2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage is an early trigger for cryoprecipitate
Tocolysis contraindicated in active abruption; oxytocin augmentation contraindicated when delivery is not imminent
explanation.pearls: Peripartum fibrinogen normally rises to 4-6 g/L; a fibrinogen <2 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage predicts progression to massive haemorrhage and is an early cryoprecipitate trigger.

options.rationale: The primary problem here is placental abruption at term with active bleeding, contractions and non-reassuring fetal patterns tending to deteriorate. Delaying delivery for magnesium prophylaxis exposes both mother and fetus to further catastrophic haemorrhage. If gestational hypertension had progressed to severe pre-eclampsia with imminent eclampsia signs, magnesium would be part of management but does not delay delivery in an active abruption. (Source: RANZCOG APH)
Tocolysis is contraindicated in active abruption because it may worsen bleeding and delay definitive delivery. It is not part of the management pathway. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

Suspected placental abruption at 36+4 weeks with active bleeding, tender firm uterus, contractions and fetal compromise warrants urgent delivery. At term or near-term with fetal or maternal compromise, this is by caesarean unless vaginal delivery is genuinely imminent. Two large-bore IV cannulae, cross-match, coagulation studies, MTP awareness (Hb 108, likely underestimates true loss, fibrinogen still normal but consumption risk is high) and neonatal team activation are the concurrent steps. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

TXA and urinary catheterisation are useful adjuncts, but a 30-minute wait for reassessment is unsafe in the presence of active abruption with fetal compromise and heavy loss. Delivery should not be delayed. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

Oxytocin augmentation in a bleeding, abrupting uterus at 3 cm cervical dilation without fetal head deep in the pelvis is dangerous and takes hours to achieve delivery. Category 1 caesarean is the safest route. (Source: RANZCOG APH)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum with strong antenatal ultrasound features (lacunae, myometrial thinning, bladder wall bulging, hypervascularity) in the setting of prior caesarean plus praevia is managed by planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a tertiary centre. Multidisciplinary team includes maternal-fetal medicine, interventional radiology, urology, senior anaesthesia, neonatology and blood bank. Standard operative approach is caesarean-hysterectomy with placenta left in situ rather than attempted removal.
key_points: Placenta accreta spectrum: deliver 34+0 to 35+6 weeks by planned caesarean at tertiary centre
Multidisciplinary team: MFM, IR, urology, senior anaesthesia, senior neonatology, blood bank
Standard operation: caesarean-hysterectomy with placenta left in situ (do not attempt removal)
Pre-optimise iron; antenatal corticosteroids for preterm delivery; consider cell salvage
explanation.pearls: Sensitivity of ultrasound plus colour Doppler for placenta accreta approaches 90% in high-volume centres; MRI adds most value for suspected posterior placentation or when depth of invasion (percreta) is unclear.

options.rationale: Placenta praevia with strong ultrasound features of placenta accreta spectrum absolutely contraindicates a vaginal delivery attempt because of catastrophic haemorrhage risk. Delivery is by planned caesarean at a tertiary centre. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

Placenta accreta spectrum requires multidisciplinary tertiary-centre management. Regional facilities without interventional radiology, cell salvage, immediate blood products and colorectal or urological backup are the wrong setting, and delivery timing at 39 weeks is too late. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

Attempted forced placental removal in placenta accreta spectrum precipitates massive haemorrhage. The standard approach when accreta is confirmed is caesarean-hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ, or occasionally a conservative leave-in-situ approach in highly selected cases. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

Delivery at 32 weeks is earlier than recommended when the mother is stable and asymptomatic; RANZCOG recommends 34+0 to 35+6 weeks for suspected placenta accreta spectrum unless bleeding, contractions, or fetal compromise force earlier delivery. Antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium neuroprotection should also be given for planned preterm delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

Suspected placenta accreta spectrum with strong ultrasound features and prior caesarean history should be delivered by planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a tertiary centre with a dedicated multidisciplinary team. Standard care includes antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity, planned caesarean-hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ (preferred to piecemeal removal), interventional radiology for possible internal iliac balloon occlusion, urology on standby for possible bladder involvement, cell salvage, and pre-optimisation of iron stores. RANZCOG endorses this pathway. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta accreta spectrum)

explanation.summary: Quintero staging for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome: Stage I (donor DVP <2 cm with recipient DVP >8 cm before 20 weeks or >10 cm after 20 weeks), Stage II (bladder not visualised in donor for at least 60 minutes), Stage III (abnormal Doppler in either twin), Stage IV (hydrops in either twin), Stage V (in utero demise of one or both twins). Stage II or higher between 16 and 26 weeks is treated with fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses at a fetal therapy centre. Eurofetus RCT showed superiority over amnioreduction.
key_points: Quintero Stage II TTTS: oligohydramnios donor, polyhydramnios recipient, donor bladder not visualised in 60 min
Fetoscopic laser ablation for Stage II or higher between 16-26 weeks is standard of care
Eurofetus RCT: laser at least one twin survival 76% vs amnioreduction 51%; better neurological outcomes at 6 months
Amnioreduction reserved for beyond treatable window or centre inaccessibility
explanation.pearls: Australian fetal therapy is centralised (Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane) and referral is national; treating within Quintero Stage II or III before hydrops onset offers best neurodevelopmental outcomes.

options.rationale: This is Quintero Stage II twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome: oligohydramnios in donor (DVP 2 cm at 20 weeks; less than 2 cm is required for stage I; combined with non-visualised bladder over 60 minutes moves to Stage II), polyhydramnios in recipient (DVP >8 cm before 20 weeks or >10 cm after 20 weeks). Stage II or higher TTTS between 16 and 26 weeks is managed with fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses, which improves at least one twin survival from 33% (amnioreduction alone) to 76% (Eurofetus and Solomon trials). Australian fetal therapy is centralised at select tertiary centres and urgent referral today is essential to allow assessment and intervention within the treatable window. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

Serial amnioreduction has substantially inferior outcomes to fetoscopic laser for Stage II or higher TTTS between 16 and 26 weeks (Eurofetus trial: laser survival benefit sustained at 6 months). It is retained as a temporising measure only when laser is not available or the woman is beyond the treatable gestational window. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

Once Quintero Stage II is reached, intervention improves outcomes substantially. Waiting for Doppler abnormalities allows progression to Stage III or IV where perinatal outcomes are markedly worse. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

Selective feticide is reserved for cases with impending demise of one twin or where laser is contraindicated or unsuccessful. It is not first-line when fetoscopic laser remains a treatment option. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

Delivery at 20 weeks is not survivable. Delivery for TTTS is planned around 34 to 37 weeks after successful in utero treatment, unless earlier for obstetric or fetal reasons. (Source: RANZCOG Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia (BP >=160/110, symptoms, heavy proteinuria) at or beyond 34 weeks requires acute BP control with IV labetalol or hydralazine, magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis (4 g IV load then 1 g/hour), and planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours. Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity are not indicated after 34+0 weeks. Vaginal delivery is preferred when maternal and fetal status allow. Continuous CTG and strict fluid balance limited to 80 mL/hour reduce pulmonary oedema risk.
key_points: Severe BP threshold: >=160/110 mmHg treated with IV labetalol 20 to 40 mg or IV hydralazine 5 to 10 mg
Magnesium sulfate loading 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis
Delivery within 24 to 48 hours at or beyond 34+0 weeks with severe features
Fluid restriction 80 mL/hour to avoid pulmonary oedema
explanation.pearls: Target BP after treatment is 140 to 150 / 80 to 100 mmHg to avoid placental hypoperfusion; overshoot toward normotension in a chronically hypertensive placenta can cause acute fetal distress.

options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia at 34+ weeks with severe hypertension, symptoms and heavy proteinuria requires acute BP control (IV labetalol 20 to 40 mg or IV hydralazine), magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis, and planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours after corticosteroid completion is not required after 34+0. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia (>=160/110 mmHg) requires rapid IV or fast-acting oral treatment to lower BP within 15 to 30 minutes; oral labetalol 12-hourly is too slow. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Immediate delivery without prior BP control risks maternal stroke; acute treatment of severe hypertension precedes and continues through delivery. Vaginal delivery is not contraindicated when maternal and fetal condition allow. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Sublingual nifedipine causes precipitous BP drop and is not used in pre-eclampsia; discharge is unsafe given severe features (BP, symptoms, proteinuria) requiring inpatient monitoring and delivery planning. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Furosemide is not first line and reduces already contracted intravascular volume in pre-eclampsia. Methyldopa is safe in pregnancy but its onset is slow and unsuitable for severe hypertension requiring rapid control. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Low-dose aspirin (100 to 150 mg nocte, 150 mg preferred) started between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks and continued until 36+0 weeks reduces the risk of pre-eclampsia by approximately 60 percent when started in early pregnancy in high-risk women. High-risk factors include prior PET, chronic hypertension, chronic kidney disease, pre-existing diabetes, and autoimmune disease. Two or more moderate risk factors (nulliparity, age >=40, BMI >=35, family history, IVF, multiple pregnancy interval) also indicate prophylaxis. The window is critical: starting after 16 weeks loses much of the benefit.
key_points: Start aspirin 100 to 150 mg at night between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks
Continue until 36+0 weeks (stop before delivery to reduce bleeding risk)
High-risk indication: prior PET, chronic HTN, CKD, diabetes, autoimmune disease
Calcium supplementation is second line in low-dietary-calcium populations
explanation.pearls: Aspirin 150 mg reduces preterm PET by approximately 62 percent (ASPRE trial 2017); the effect at term PET is smaller. Timing (before 16+0) matters more than dose within the 100 to 150 mg range.

options.rationale: Aspirin started after 16+0 weeks has substantially reduced benefit for PET prevention because trophoblast invasion is largely complete. Starting between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks gives maximal benefit. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

SOMANZ and RANZCOG recommend low-dose aspirin (100 to 150 mg nocte, current evidence favours 150 mg) started between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks and continued until 36 to 37 weeks in women with one or more high-risk factors (prior PET, chronic HTN, CKD, autoimmune disease, diabetes) OR two or more moderate risk factors. This patient has two high-risk factors. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Calcium supplementation reduces PET risk primarily in women with low dietary calcium intake. In an Australian setting with adequate calcium intake, aspirin is the preferred prophylaxis in high-risk women. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Sodium restriction does not reduce PET risk and may worsen intravascular volume depletion. This patient has clear indications for aspirin prophylaxis given prior PET plus chronic HTN. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

LMWH is not indicated for PET prevention alone; its use in pregnancy is for VTE prophylaxis or antiphospholipid syndrome. Aspirin is the correct choice for PET prophylaxis in this patient. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Moderate to severe hyperemesis gravidarum (PUQE >=13, weight loss >5 percent, ketonuria, electrolyte disturbance) requires admission for IV rehydration with normal saline plus potassium and stepped antiemetic therapy: pyridoxine plus doxylamine, ondansetron (first trimester use is now considered safe in most guidance), metoclopramide. Thiamine 100 mg IV must precede any dextrose containing fluid to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory disease after 10 weeks.
key_points: IV normal saline with potassium; avoid initial dextrose without prior thiamine
Thiamine 100 mg IV before any glucose load in prolonged vomiting
Stepped antiemetics: pyridoxine + doxylamine, then ondansetron or metoclopramide
PUQE score categorises severity (mild <7, moderate 7 to 12, severe >=13)
explanation.pearls: Ondansetron in the first trimester carries a small absolute cardiac malformation signal (approximately 3 additional cases per 10,000 exposures) balanced against the harms of untreated severe hyperemesis; RANZCOG considers benefit outweighs risk with informed consent.

options.rationale: This patient has severe dehydration, hypokalaemia, ketonuria and metabolic alkalosis; discharge is unsafe. Admission for IV rehydration is warranted before oral therapy is likely to work. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

Dextrose without preceding thiamine risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy in prolonged vomiting. Normal saline with potassium is preferred first, and thiamine must be given before any glucose load. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

Moderate to severe hyperemesis with dehydration and hypokalaemia requires IV rehydration with normal saline (avoid dextrose containing solutions initially) plus potassium replacement. Thiamine 100 mg IV must precede any dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Add pyridoxine plus doxylamine and second-line antiemetic (ondansetron or metoclopramide) as pharmacotherapy. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

Corticosteroids are considered only after failure of stepped pharmacotherapy including pyridoxine plus doxylamine, ondansetron and metoclopramide, and are avoided before 10 weeks due to a small oral cleft signal. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

There are no neurological signs or atypical features to suggest raised intracranial pressure; investigations for secondary causes are reserved for unusual features. Empiric treatment for hyperemesis is appropriate here. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

explanation.summary: IV iron in pregnancy is indicated after the first trimester when oral iron fails, is not tolerated, or when replenishment before delivery is needed (typically >28 weeks with iron deficiency anaemia). Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes and ferric derisomaltose 20 mg/kg allow single-dose replacement; iron sucrose requires multiple 200 mg doses. Anaphylaxis risk is very low with modern formulations but resuscitation facilities must be available. Oral iron alternate day dosing improves absorption over daily dosing (hepcidin biology).
key_points: IV iron indications: oral failure, intolerance, non-adherence, need for rapid correction >28 weeks
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes as single outpatient dose
Ferric derisomaltose 20 mg/kg alternative (higher single dose cap)
Transfusion reserved for Hb <70 or haemodynamic compromise
explanation.pearls: Hypophosphataemia after ferric carboxymaltose is common (approximately 40 percent) and may cause fatigue or bone pain; check phosphate 2 to 4 weeks post-infusion if symptomatic. Ferric derisomaltose has lower hypophosphataemia risk.

options.rationale: Recent evidence favours alternate day dosing over multiple daily doses (hepcidin rise blocks absorption). She has documented intolerance; escalating is unlikely to succeed and IV iron is indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic severe anaemia (Hb <70), haemodynamic compromise, or ongoing bleeding. Hb 92 with iron deficiency responds to IV iron with lower risk than transfusion. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

Dietary iron alone cannot correct established iron deficiency anaemia at 30 weeks with ferritin 8 in the required timeframe before delivery. Active replacement is required. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

IV iron is indicated for iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy after 13 weeks when oral iron fails, is not tolerated, or when rapid replenishment is needed (>28 weeks with anaemia). Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV as a single dose is convenient and effective; ferric derisomaltose (Monofer) is an alternative. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

Intramuscular iron is not routinely used in pregnancy (staining, pain, unreliable absorption). Iron sucrose IV requires multiple visits; ferric carboxymaltose or ferric derisomaltose allow single-dose replacement. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated because 20 to 40 percent progress to pyelonephritis and there is an association with preterm birth. Nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 5 days is first line in the second trimester; cefalexin 500 mg 6-hourly for 5 days is an alternative. Nitrofurantoin is avoided at term (34 weeks onward) and near delivery because of neonatal haemolysis risk. Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester due to folate antagonism. A test of cure MSU is performed 1 to 2 weeks after treatment.
key_points: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy to prevent pyelonephritis and preterm birth
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO 6-hourly for 5 days first line in second trimester
Avoid nitrofurantoin from 34 weeks onward (neonatal haemolysis)
Test of cure MSU 1 to 2 weeks after treatment
explanation.pearls: In G6PD deficiency, nitrofurantoin causes haemolysis at any gestation. In this cohort choose cefalexin 500 mg 6-hourly for 5 days or amoxicillin plus clavulanate 500/125 mg 8-hourly (based on susceptibility) instead.

options.rationale: Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester (folate antagonism, neural tube defect signal) and generally not used in pregnancy unless no alternative. At 14 weeks it is second choice. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

Fosfomycin single dose is an option in non-pregnant women but is not first line in Australian pregnancy guidance where 5 to 7 day treatment courses are recommended. Nitrofurantoin remains first line in the second trimester. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy warrants treatment because up to 30 to 40 percent progress to pyelonephritis without therapy, and bacteriuria is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

Amoxicillin resistance in community E. coli is around 50 percent even with reported susceptibility on some panels; nitrofurantoin or cefalexin are preferred first-line agents in pregnancy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated to reduce pyelonephritis (60 percent risk if untreated) and preterm birth. Nitrofurantoin is first line in the second trimester (avoid at term and near delivery due to neonatal haemolysis risk). Duration is 5 to 7 days and a test of cure MSU is performed 1 to 2 weeks later. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: After suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole, serum beta hCG is monitored weekly until three consecutive normal results, then monthly for 6 months. Effective contraception (COCP or barrier) is used to prevent pregnancy that would confound surveillance; IUD is avoided until hCG is normal. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia develops in 15 to 20 percent of complete moles and requires methotrexate or actinomycin D. Referral to a specialist GTD service is recommended.
key_points: Weekly beta hCG until 3 normal results then monthly for 6 months (complete mole)
Partial mole: weekly until 3 normal then discharge
Effective contraception during surveillance; avoid IUD until hCG normal
15 to 20 percent of complete moles develop GTN needing chemotherapy
explanation.pearls: FIGO criteria for GTN after mole: hCG plateau over 4 measurements 3 weeks apart, hCG rise >=10 percent over 3 measurements 2 weeks apart, hCG persisting >=6 months after evacuation, or histological choriocarcinoma.

options.rationale: Complete mole surveillance is weekly serum beta hCG until three consecutive normal results then monthly for 6 months. Effective contraception (COCP or condoms; avoid IUD until hCG normal) prevents pregnancy that would confound hCG surveillance and delay recognition of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

Surveillance is essential to detect GTN, which affects 15 to 20 percent of complete moles and 1 to 5 percent of partial moles. Missing follow-up delays chemotherapy for treatable disease. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)
Prophylactic chemotherapy is not routinely recommended; surveillance identifies those needing treatment and avoids unnecessary chemotherapy in most patients. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

IUD insertion is deferred until beta hCG has normalised, as insertion trauma and rare uterine perforation of residual disease raise concerns about persistence detection and haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)
Staging imaging is performed when GTN is diagnosed (plateau or rise in hCG, histological features) not routinely after evacuation of a mole with expected declining hCG. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

explanation.summary: Delivery timing in twins is guided by chorionicity: dichorionic diamniotic at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks; monochorionic diamniotic at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks; monochorionic monoamniotic by caesarean at 32+0 to 34+0 weeks. Mode of delivery is guided by presentation and fetal status; vaginal birth is appropriate when the leading twin is cephalic and there are no contraindications. Continuous CTG in labour and early recourse to caesarean for the second twin are standard. Second twin non-cephalic delivery may be by breech extraction or internal podalic version with an experienced operator.
key_points: MCDA delivery 36+0 to 36+6 weeks (uncomplicated)
DCDA delivery 37+0 to 37+6 weeks (uncomplicated)
MCMA delivery by caesarean 32+0 to 34+0 weeks with steroids
Vaginal birth if leading twin cephalic and no contraindications
explanation.pearls: Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks in MCDA/MCMA for early detection of TTTS, TAPS and sIUGR; DCDA scans 4-weekly. Discordance >20 percent EFW warrants closer surveillance and consideration of delivery.

options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends delivery of uncomplicated MCDA twins between 36+0 and 36+6 weeks because of the increased stillbirth risk beyond 37 weeks. Vaginal birth is appropriate when the leading twin is cephalic and there are no obstetric or fetal contraindications. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

Continuing beyond 37 weeks in MCDA twins increases perinatal mortality. The stillbirth risk in monochorionic pregnancy rises earlier than in dichorionic, so delivery is planned earlier. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

Monochorionicity alone is not an indication for caesarean when both twins are appropriately grown and the leading twin is cephalic. Vaginal birth is preferred when feasible. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

Dichorionic twins are delivered at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks; monochorionic diamniotic at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks; monochorionic monoamniotic by caesarean at 32+0 to 34+0 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

Monochorionic monoamniotic (MCMA) twins are delivered by caesarean at 32 to 34 weeks. MCDA are delivered later (36+0 to 36+6). Confusing the two chorionicities is a common error. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Decreased fetal movements at or beyond 28 weeks warrant prompt assessment with continuous CTG for at least 20 minutes plus ultrasound for growth, amniotic fluid volume, and Doppler within 24 hours (particularly if this is a first episode or there are risk factors). Kick charts are not routinely recommended. The Safer Baby Bundle (PSANZ) standardises response and has been associated with reduced stillbirth rates in Australia. Recurrent DFM prompts consideration of delivery from 39+0 weeks even if surveillance is reassuring.
key_points: CTG for at least 20 minutes plus ultrasound within 24 hours
Kick charts not routinely recommended
Safer Baby Bundle standardises response to reduce stillbirth
Recurrent DFM: consider delivery from 39+0 weeks
explanation.pearls: Perception threshold for fetal movement counts varies widely; the pattern change (a definite decrease from a previously active baby) is more predictive than an absolute number. Sudden increase in vigorous movement also warrants assessment (uncommonly associated with cord accident).

options.rationale: RANZCOG (and PSANZ Safer Baby Bundle) recommend CTG plus growth ultrasound after any episode of decreased fetal movements at or beyond 28 weeks; discharge without assessment misses fetal compromise. Kick charts are no longer routinely recommended. (Source: RANZCOG DFM)

RANZCOG guidance on decreased fetal movements is CTG for 20 minutes minimum plus consideration of ultrasound for growth, amniotic fluid volume, and umbilical Doppler within 24 hours if this is the first episode or with any risk factors. The Safer Baby Bundle standardises this response. (Source: RANZCOG DFM)

Delivery is triggered by evidence of fetal compromise on CTG or ultrasound, not by the symptom alone. Empirical delivery exposes mother and baby to preterm and surgical risks unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCOG DFM)
Provocative measures (sweet drinks, side-lying) are not evidence based and delay assessment. Present-day RANZCOG guidance is prompt CTG and imaging as needed. (Source: RANZCOG DFM)

Steroids and delivery are not empirically triggered by decreased fetal movements alone. Assessment must confirm fetal compromise or growth restriction before this pathway is chosen. (Source: RANZCOG DFM)

explanation.summary: Routine anti-D prophylaxis for RhD negative non-sensitised women in Australia is 625 IU IM at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks (two-dose regimen), or a single 1500 IU dose at 28 weeks. Post-delivery dose within 72 hours if baby is RhD positive, adjusted by Kleihauer for fetomaternal haemorrhage. Additional doses for sensitising events: 250 IU IM for events before 12 weeks, 625 IU for events 12 to 20 weeks, and 625 IU with Kleihauer testing for events after 20 weeks.
key_points: Routine: 625 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks OR single 1500 IU at 28 weeks
Post-delivery: within 72 hours if baby RhD positive, adjusted by Kleihauer
First trimester sensitising event: 250 IU
Sensitising event 12 to 20 weeks: 625 IU
explanation.pearls: Kleihauer estimates fetal cells per 5 mL maternal blood; additional anti-D 125 IU per mL of fetomaternal haemorrhage above 6 mL. For large FMH give IV anti-D preparations for faster absorption if available.

options.rationale: The single-dose regimen gives 1500 IU at 28 weeks, not 34 weeks. A post-delivery dose adjusted by Kleihauer is essential if baby is RhD positive to prevent sensitisation from fetomaternal haemorrhage at birth. (Source: NBA Anti-D)

Routine antenatal anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks (or single 1500 IU at 28 weeks) reduces sensitisation from silent fetomaternal haemorrhage. This is standard care in Australia irrespective of sensitising events. (Source: NBA Anti-D)

Australian NBA guidance for RhD negative non-sensitised women is routine anti-D 625 IU IM at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks (two-dose regimen; a single 1500 IU dose at 28 weeks is an alternative). Post-delivery dose is given within 72 hours if baby is RhD positive, adjusted by Kleihauer. Additional doses are given after sensitising events. (Source: NBA Anti-D)

Paternal group is not reliable enough to alter management because paternity may be uncertain and cell-free fetal DNA typing is not yet routine in Australia. Prophylaxis is given based on maternal RhD alone. (Source: NBA Anti-D)

The 250 IU dose is used for first-trimester sensitising events; routine antenatal prophylaxis in the second half of pregnancy is 625 IU or single 1500 IU. Monthly dosing is not standard. (Source: NBA Anti-D)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is managed using the HELPERR mnemonic: call for Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs into McRoberts (hyperflexion of hips to abdomen), suprapubic Pressure (downward and lateral toward the anterior shoulder to disimpact from symphysis), internal Enter manoeuvres (Rubin II rotation of anterior shoulder, Woods screw of posterior shoulder), Remove posterior arm, Roll onto all fours (Gaskin manoeuvre). McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves 50 to 60 percent of cases. Zavanelli, symphysiotomy, or Cleidotomy are last resort. Fundal pressure is contraindicated.
key_points: HELPERR mnemonic: Help, Evaluate, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter, Remove, Roll
McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure resolves 50 to 60 percent of cases
AVOID fundal pressure (worsens impaction, uterine rupture risk)
AVOID downward traction on fetal head (brachial plexus injury)
explanation.pearls: Time is critical to reduce hypoxic injury and Erb's palsy risk; document minutes from head delivery, manoeuvres attempted with times, staff present, and cord gases postnatally. Debrief and formal clinical review afterward reduces medicolegal risk.

options.rationale: Zavanelli (cephalic replacement and caesarean) is a last-resort manoeuvre after failed conventional efforts. First-line is McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia because it worsens impaction and can cause uterine rupture. Suprapubic pressure (above the symphysis directed toward the anterior shoulder) is used. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

Episiotomy alone does not resolve shoulder dystocia (a bony problem) and downward traction risks brachial plexus injury. Manoeuvres to disimpact the shoulder are required. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

The HELPERR mnemonic starts with H (call for Help), E (evaluate for episiotomy), L (Legs into McRoberts), P (suprapubic Pressure), E (Enter manoeuvres: Rubin II, Woods screw), R (Remove posterior arm), R (Roll onto all fours). McRoberts alone or with suprapubic pressure resolves 50 to 60 percent of dystocias. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

Augmenting contractions does not overcome a bony impaction and risks worsening injury. The problem requires positional and manual manoeuvres, not more contractions. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program screens women aged 25 to 74 with primary HPV testing every 5 years. Self-collection has been available to all screening participants since July 2022 and is analytically equivalent to clinician-collected samples for HPV testing (but does not allow reflex cytology on the same sample, requiring recall for cytology if HPV positive not 16/18). HPV 16 or 18 positive triggers direct colposcopy referral; other HR HPV positive triggers reflex cytology on the sample. Exit test at 70 to 74 if two consecutive normal screens.
key_points: Primary HPV test every 5 years, ages 25 to 74
Self-collection available to all since July 2022
HPV 16/18 positive: direct colposcopy
Other HR HPV positive: reflex cytology
explanation.pearls: Self-collected samples require recall for a clinician-collected sample if HPV positive (not 16/18) because cytology cannot be performed on self-collected specimens. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women are strongly encouraged to participate in screening; self-collection may improve engagement.

options.rationale: The Australian program switched from Pap cytology every 2 years to primary HPV testing every 5 years for ages 25 to 74 in December 2017. Cytology alone is no longer the primary screening test. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

Reflex cytology is only triggered by an HPV-positive result (except HPV 16 or 18 which triggers direct colposcopy). Annual screening is not recommended in a healthy vaccinated 25-year-old. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)
HPV vaccination reduces but does not eliminate cervical cancer risk (vaccines cover 9 high-risk types but not all). Screening starts at 25 regardless of vaccination status. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)
Colposcopy is not a screening test; it is used for triage of HPV-positive results (particularly types 16/18) or after abnormal cytology. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

The Australian National Cervical Screening Program (NCSP) uses primary HPV testing every 5 years for women aged 25 to 74. Since July 2022, self-collection has been available to all screening participants; it is analytically equivalent to clinician-collected samples for HPV testing. Return interval is 5 years if HPV negative. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: First-line therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding without structural cause and where contraception is acceptable is the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS 52 mg, Mirena), which reduces menstrual blood loss by 70 to 95 percent and provides 5 years of highly effective contraception. Alternatives include tranexamic acid 1 g PO 6-hourly on bleeding days (non-hormonal, non-contraceptive), COCP (contraceptive), and cyclic oral progestogens (higher failure rate). Endometrial ablation and hysterectomy are second-line surgical options after failed medical therapy. Structural cause (fibroid, polyp, adenomyosis, malignancy) is excluded before assuming primary HMB.
key_points: LNG-IUS first line for HMB without structural cause
Tranexamic acid 1 g QID during bleeding: non-hormonal alternative
Ablation second line after medical failure
Hysterectomy is definitive last resort
explanation.pearls: Endometrial biopsy is indicated in HMB with age >=45, persistent bleeding despite treatment, or risk factors for endometrial cancer (obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen use, family history of Lynch syndrome).

options.rationale: NICE and RANZCOG recommend the LNG-IUS (Mirena 52 mg) as first-line for HMB without structural cause when contraception is acceptable. It reduces menstrual blood loss by 70 to 95 percent, corrects anaemia, and offers 5 years of contraception. Other options (tranexamic acid, COCP) are second line if LNG-IUS declined. (Source: RANZCOG HMB)

Ablation is second line after failed medical therapy in HMB without structural cause. Medical therapy (LNG-IUS first) is preferred initial treatment. Ablation is not contraceptive and pregnancy after ablation is high risk. (Source: RANZCOG HMB)
Hysterectomy is definitive but is a last resort after failed medical and less invasive surgical options. It is not first-line for HMB with normal uterus and completed family. (Source: RANZCOG HMB)
Iron replacement is important adjunct but does not treat the HMB. Waiting 12 months delays effective therapy while ongoing bleeding perpetuates anaemia. (Source: RANZCOG HMB)

GnRH agonists are used short-term before surgery or to control severe symptoms; they cause menopausal symptoms and bone loss so long-term use requires add-back HRT. They are not first-line for uncomplicated HMB. (Source: RANZCOG HMB)

explanation.summary: Postnatal contraception timing depends on breastfeeding status and time from birth. Combined hormonal contraception is category 4 until 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women (VTE risk plus milk supply) and category 3 from 6 weeks to 6 months breastfeeding; category 3 until 3 weeks and category 2 from 3 to 6 weeks postpartum in non-breastfeeding women. Progestogen-only methods (POP, DMPA, implant, LNG-IUS) are category 1 to 2 from 21 days postpartum regardless of breastfeeding. Copper IUD from 4 weeks (or immediately post-placenta with expulsion risk).
key_points: COC: category 4 breastfeeding < 6 weeks; category 3 breastfeeding 6 weeks to 6 months
POP, DMPA, implant, LNG-IUS: from 21 days postpartum any status
Cu IUD or LNG-IUS: from 4 weeks postpartum (or immediately post-placenta)
LAM alone: only if <6 months, exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic
explanation.pearls: Fertility returns approximately 6 weeks after birth in non-breastfeeding women; earlier fertility return is possible so contraception should be discussed before discharge from hospital, not left to the 6 week check.

options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC/AUMEC category 4 (unacceptable risk) until 6 weeks postpartum if breastfeeding, and category 3 (risks usually outweigh benefits) from 6 weeks to 6 months in breastfeeding women, because of VTE risk and reduced milk supply. Not appropriate here. (Source: WHO MEC Contraception)

Progestogen-only methods (POP, DMPA, implant, LNG-IUS) can be started from 21 days postpartum in breastfeeding women; UKMEC/AUMEC category 1 to 2. They do not affect breast milk supply or contain estrogen. (Source: WHO MEC Contraception)

Progestogen-only methods are safe from 21 days postpartum in breastfeeding women. Barriers alone have higher failure rates. Lactational amenorrhoea method has strict criteria and only lasts 6 months. (Source: WHO MEC Contraception)

Copper IUD can be inserted from 4 weeks postpartum but she has stated a preference for oral hormonal contraception. POP meets her needs. IUD insertion between 48 hours and 4 weeks postpartum is associated with increased expulsion. (Source: WHO MEC Contraception)
DMPA is a reasonable option but she prefers oral. Progestogen-only pill fits her preferences and can start today. Complex sequencing is not needed. (Source: WHO MEC Contraception)

explanation.summary: Threatened miscarriage is per vaginal bleeding in pregnancy with a closed cervix and a live intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound. When fetal heart is present at 8 weeks, approximately 95 percent of pregnancies continue. Management is expectant with safety-net advice (increasing bleeding, severe pain, faintness, fever, or loss of pregnancy symptoms). Progesterone is considered in women with a history of previous miscarriage (PRISM trial). RhD negative women receive anti-D 250 IU IM only after specific first-trimester sensitising events, not for spontaneous bleeding alone.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage with live IUP at 8 weeks: ~95 percent continue
Expectant management with safety-net advice
Progesterone only if history of previous miscarriage(s)
Anti-D in T1 for RhD negative only after specific sensitising events
explanation.pearls: Beta hCG serial testing (48-hour doubling) is used when ultrasound is inconclusive; a rise of at least 53 percent over 48 hours is expected in viable IUP under 6+3 weeks. Above discriminatory hCG (2000 IU/L) an intrauterine sac should be visible on TVUS.

options.rationale: PRISM trial supports vaginal progesterone in women with threatened miscarriage AND previous miscarriage(s); benefit in first-episode threatened miscarriage without prior loss is small. Empiric use in every case is not recommended in Australia. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss)
Bed rest does not reduce miscarriage rates and daily ultrasounds provide no additional useful information. Neither is recommended. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss)

Threatened miscarriage with a live intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound has approximately 95 percent chance of continuing when the fetal heart rate is confirmed at 8 weeks. Management is expectant with safety-net advice. Anti-D is not required in the first trimester unless there is a specific sensitising event (surgical management, therapeutic termination, ectopic surgery). (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss)

There is a live pregnancy on ultrasound; there is no indication for surgical intervention. Threatened miscarriage with live embryo continues in 95 percent of cases. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss)

The patient is not Rh negative so anti-D is not required. Anti-D in the first trimester is given for RhD negative women only after specific sensitising events (miscarriage requiring surgical management, therapeutic termination, ectopic surgery, chorionic villus sampling). (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss)

explanation.summary: Vulvovaginal candidiasis in pregnancy is treated with topical imidazoles (clotrimazole 100 mg pessary nightly for 6 nights, or 200 mg for 3 nights, plus vulval cream). Oral fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy because of miscarriage and cardiac malformation signals (particularly at doses of 400 mg per day or more). Recurrence is common in pregnancy; a longer 7-day course is preferred over single-dose or 3-day therapy. Recurrent (>=4 episodes per year) or resistant candidiasis prompts culture and sensitivity because non-albicans species (glabrata, krusei) require different agents.
key_points: Topical clotrimazole pessary 100 mg nightly for 6 nights (or 200 mg x 3 nights) in pregnancy
Avoid oral fluconazole and other oral azoles in pregnancy
Longer course preferred in pregnancy due to recurrence risk
Culture if recurrent or resistant (non-albicans species need different treatment)
explanation.pearls: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (>=4 episodes per year) outside of pregnancy is treated with induction (fluconazole 150 mg every 72 hours for 3 doses) then maintenance (fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months). This regimen is not used in pregnancy.

options.rationale: Oral fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy: any-dose exposure is associated with a small spontaneous abortion signal and 400 mg/day plus exposure with tetralogy of Fallot and other malformations. Topical treatment is preferred throughout pregnancy. (Source: eTG Genital Candidiasis)
Oral azoles including itraconazole are category B3 in pregnancy and generally avoided. Topical clotrimazole is preferred and effective. (Source: eTG Genital Candidiasis)
Boric acid is contraindicated in pregnancy (embryotoxicity and no reliable safety data). It is reserved for resistant non-albicans species in non-pregnant patients. (Source: eTG Genital Candidiasis)

In pregnancy, topical imidazoles (clotrimazole, miconazole) are first line for vulvovaginal candidiasis; a 7-day course (100 mg nightly or 200 mg for 3 nights) is preferred because pregnancy-related recurrence is common with shorter courses. Oral fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy because of cardiac malformation and spontaneous abortion signals. (Source: eTG Genital Candidiasis)
Topical corticosteroid alone does not treat candidiasis; it will worsen the infection and provides only transient symptom masking. Antifungal is required. (Source: eTG Genital Candidiasis)

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy because they cause fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, IUGR, and neonatal hypotension in the second and third trimesters, and carry cardiac and CNS malformation signals in the first trimester. Cease at pregnancy confirmation. First-line pregnancy antihypertensives are labetalol (100 to 400 mg BD or TDS), methyldopa (250 to 500 mg TDS), and nifedipine slow release (30 to 60 mg daily). Target BP in chronic HTN in pregnancy is <140/90 (CHIPS trial supports tight control). Atenolol is avoided (IUGR). Thiazides reduce plasma volume.
key_points: ACEi and ARBs contraindicated across pregnancy; cease at confirmation
First line: labetalol, methyldopa, nifedipine SR
Target BP <140/90 in chronic HTN in pregnancy (CHIPS)
Avoid atenolol (IUGR) and thiazides (volume depletion)
explanation.pearls: Aspirin 100 to 150 mg nocte from 12 to 16 weeks reduces pre-eclampsia risk by ~60 percent in high-risk women (chronic HTN, prior PET, CKD, autoimmune, diabetes). This patient has a clear indication.

options.rationale: ACE inhibitors and ARBs cause fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, IUGR and neonatal hypotension, and are contraindicated in second and third trimester; first trimester exposure carries cardiac and CNS malformation signals. Cease as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)
ACEi carry first-trimester malformation signals (cardiac, CNS), so early switch is preferred. Continuing exposure through T1 adds unnecessary risk. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Thiazides are generally avoided in pregnancy because they reduce plasma volume and can worsen placental hypoperfusion; first-line pregnancy antihypertensives are labetalol, methyldopa, and slow-release nifedipine. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)
Atenolol is associated with IUGR and is generally avoided in pregnancy. Labetalol is a preferred alpha and beta blocker with a better fetal safety profile. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated across pregnancy; cease at diagnosis of pregnancy and switch to a pregnancy-safe antihypertensive: labetalol first line, methyldopa alternative, nifedipine slow release as third option. Target BP is <140/90 in chronic HTN in pregnancy. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Suspected choledocholithiasis in pregnancy is investigated with MRCP (no ionising radiation) and treated with ERCP plus sphincterotomy under fluoroscopy with lead shielding of the fetus if confirmed. Interval laparoscopic cholecystectomy is planned, ideally in the second trimester (T2 is the safest window: T1 has organogenesis concerns; T3 has surgical access and preterm labour risk). Delay of definitive treatment risks cholangitis and gallstone pancreatitis. Uncomplicated biliary colic can be managed conservatively but recurrent symptoms indicate cholecystectomy.
key_points: MRCP first line (no ionising radiation) for suspected CBD stones in pregnancy
ERCP with lead shielding for confirmed choledocholithiasis
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy ideally in T2 (safest window)
Do not delay treatment (cholangitis, pancreatitis risks)
explanation.pearls: Gallstone disease is 2 to 3 times more common in pregnancy due to elevated estrogen (increased cholesterol saturation) and reduced gallbladder motility (progesterone). Ursodeoxycholic acid does not resolve established stones but is used in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy for symptom relief.

options.rationale: MRCP is safe in pregnancy (no ionising radiation) and diagnostic for CBD stones. If confirmed, ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is performed with lead shielding of the fetus and minimised fluoroscopy time. Interval laparoscopic cholecystectomy is planned, ideally in T2 (safest window). (Source: RANZCOG Medical Disorders)

Direct surgery without confirming CBD stone is unnecessary. MRCP is diagnostic and non-invasive; ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is preferred for CBD stones in pregnancy. Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy is planned after ERCP, ideally in second trimester. (Source: RANZCOG Medical Disorders)
CT exposes the fetus to ionising radiation and is less sensitive than MRCP for CBD stones. MRCP is preferred as the non-radiation alternative. (Source: RANZCOG Medical Disorders)

Delaying treatment risks ascending cholangitis, pancreatitis, and sepsis. ERCP is safe in pregnancy with lead shielding. Definitive treatment should not wait until after birth if choledocholithiasis is confirmed. (Source: RANZCOG Medical Disorders)

Delivery is not required for choledocholithiasis; it is treated with ERCP in pregnancy. Preterm delivery for a non-obstetric surgical condition adds unnecessary neonatal risk. (Source: RANZCOG Medical Disorders)

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture during TOLAC is a life-threatening emergency for mother and baby. Classical features include sudden severe suprapubic pain persisting between contractions, loss of station, fresh vaginal bleeding, prolonged fetal heart rate deceleration, maternal haemodynamic compromise, and cessation of contractions. Immediate management: stop oxytocin, IV resuscitation, cross-match 4 units, call for senior obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams, and proceed directly to category-1 laparotomy. At laparotomy the fetus is delivered rapidly and the uterus repaired if feasible, or hysterectomy performed for uncontrolled haemorrhage.
key_points: Uterine rupture: sudden severe pain, station loss, fresh PV bleed, prolonged deceleration, maternal collapse
Immediate: stop oxytocin, IV resuscitation, cross-match, cat-1 laparotomy
Do NOT delay for imaging or tocolysis
Risk in TOLAC ~0.5 to 1 percent; classical CS scar precludes VBAC
explanation.pearls: Prior classical (vertical) caesarean, T- or J-incision, or fundal uterine surgery (myomectomy involving cavity) are contraindications to VBAC because of much higher rupture risk (4 to 9 percent for classical vs 0.5 to 1 percent for LSCS).

options.rationale: Tocolysis is not appropriate when rupture is suspected. Oxytocin must be stopped and delivery expedited. Terbutaline would delay definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

The clinical picture (sudden severe pain, station loss, fresh bleeding, prolonged deceleration, maternal instability, prior CS) is highly suggestive of uterine rupture. Immediate actions: stop oxytocin, IV fluid resuscitation, cross-match blood, call for senior support, and proceed to emergency category-1 laparotomy for delivery and repair or hysterectomy. Uterine rupture in TOLAC occurs in approximately 0.5 to 1 percent of trials of labour. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

Uterine rupture is a clinical diagnosis and time to delivery is critical for fetal survival. Delaying for imaging risks fetal death and maternal exsanguination. Move to laparotomy on clinical grounds. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)
At 8 cm dilatation instrumental delivery is not possible (requires full dilatation). Suspected rupture with a high station and haemodynamic instability requires laparotomy. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)
Observation delays essential treatment. Prolonged decelerations without recovery within a few minutes, in the context of suspected rupture, mandate immediate laparotomy. (Source: RANZCOG VBAC)

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate toxicity occurs at serum levels above 3.5 mmol/L (therapeutic 2 to 3.5 mmol/L). Progressive signs: loss of DTRs (>3.5), respiratory depression (>5), cardiac conduction delay and arrest (>7). Renal impairment reduces clearance and increases toxicity risk. Immediate management: stop infusion, give 10 percent calcium gluconate 10 mL IV over 10 minutes as antagonist, check serum magnesium, monitor respiration and cardiovascular status, support airway and ventilation if needed. Adjust dose in renal impairment (halve maintenance to 0.5 g/hour and check levels every 4 hours).
key_points: Toxicity signs: loss of DTRs, RR <12, drowsiness, cardiac conduction changes
Immediate: stop infusion, calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL IV
Renal impairment: halve maintenance rate and check levels every 4 hours
Therapeutic range 2 to 3.5 mmol/L; toxicity >3.5 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: Fetal magnesium exposure at delivery can cause neonatal hypotonia, respiratory depression, and hyporeflexia; alert the neonatal team if delivery occurs within 24 hours of infusion. Magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis is loaded at 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion; some protocols use 5 g IM to each buttock plus 5 g IM every 4 hours (Pritchard regimen).

options.rationale: The features are consistent with magnesium toxicity, not opioid effect. Naloxone will not reverse magnesium and continuing infusion will worsen toxicity. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Fluid loading in pre-eclampsia risks pulmonary oedema (contracted intravascular volume with capillary leak). Continued infusion at any rate in toxicity is unsafe until level is known and toxicity resolved. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Loss of DTRs, respiratory depression (RR <12), and drowsiness in a patient on magnesium sulfate suggest toxicity, especially given reduced renal clearance (CKD, worsening creatinine, oliguria). Immediate actions: stop the infusion, give calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL IV over 10 minutes as physiological antagonist, and check serum magnesium urgently. Support ventilation if respiratory arrest. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Furosemide can cause further volume depletion and does not immediately reverse toxicity. Calcium gluconate is the direct antagonist. Furosemide is used cautiously only after infusion is stopped and antidote given. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Dialysis is reserved for severe refractory toxicity with anuria not responding to conservative measures. Stopping infusion, calcium gluconate, and supportive care are first line. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Retained placenta is defined as failure to deliver the placenta within 30 minutes of active management of the third stage (or 60 minutes of physiological management). If bleeding is active, manual removal is required earlier. Management: empty bladder, transfer to theatre, regional (spinal or epidural top-up) or general anaesthesia, manual removal, IV oxytocin infusion, prophylactic antibiotics (cefazolin plus metronidazole), tranexamic acid 1 g IV, cross-match blood, and inspect for retained products. Placenta accreta spectrum is suspected if the placenta will not separate manually.
key_points: Retained placenta: >30 min after active management (or 60 min with physiological)
Manual removal in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia
Empty bladder, IV oxytocin, prophylactic antibiotics, TXA 1 g IV
Suspect placenta accreta if placenta will not separate manually
explanation.pearls: Umbilical cord blood collection for cord gases is standard whenever there is intrapartum concern (CTG changes, meconium, shoulder dystocia); an arterial pH <7.0 or base excess <-12 supports significant intrapartum hypoxic-ischaemic injury for medicolegal documentation.

options.rationale: Intraumbilical vein oxytocin has been studied but has limited evidence of benefit and is not first line when there is active bleeding. Manual removal is the definitive treatment when the placenta has not delivered at 30 to 60 minutes with active bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

Ergometrine causes uterine contraction that can trap the placenta and worsen bleeding. Waiting further with active haemorrhage delays essential treatment. Manual removal is required. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)
Bimanual compression is for atonic PPH after placenta is delivered. Uterus cannot involute with placenta in situ. Manual removal is the correct intervention. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

Retained placenta at 30 minutes with active bleeding requires manual removal under regional (spinal or epidural top-up) or general anaesthesia. Empty the bladder first (distension impairs uterine contraction), give IV oxytocin infusion to maintain uterine tone, prophylactic antibiotics (cefazolin plus metronidazole) as intrauterine manipulation is being performed, and cross-match blood. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

Hysterectomy is a last-resort for uncontrollable haemorrhage after manual removal, bimanual compression, uterotonics, tranexamic acid, and Bakri balloon fail. It is not first-line. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

explanation.summary: Aspirin prophylaxis reduces pre-eclampsia risk by approximately 60 percent in high-risk women but does not eliminate it. New severe pre-eclampsia at 32+ weeks despite aspirin requires immediate inpatient management: acute BP control (IV labetalol or hydralazine to target <160/110 avoiding overshoot below 140/90), magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis, antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if under 34 weeks, strict fluid balance (80 mL/hour max), and planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours (after corticosteroid completion where feasible).
key_points: Severe PET features: BP >=160/110, symptoms, heavy proteinuria, low platelets, rising creatinine
Acute BP control (IV labetalol or hydralazine); target <160/110 not below 140/90
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis
Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if <34 weeks; deliver within 24 to 48 hours
explanation.pearls: PlGF/sFlt-1 ratio has entered clinical use in some centres for triage of suspected PET; a low ratio (<38) has strong negative predictive value for PET within 1 week, allowing safer outpatient monitoring.

options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia (BP >=160/110, severe symptoms, low platelets, rising creatinine, heavy proteinuria) is not managed as outpatient. Immediate inpatient care with acute BP control, magnesium sulfate, and delivery planning is required. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)
Expectant management to 37 weeks is not safe with severe pre-eclampsia features. Maternal risk (stroke, HELLP, eclampsia, renal failure) mandates earlier delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Delivery is planned within 24 to 48 hours after corticosteroids and BP stabilisation. Cat-1 CS without pre-op BP control risks maternal stroke. Cat-1 is reserved for imminent maternal or fetal risk (eclamptic seizure, abruption, non-reassuring CTG). (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Aspirin is stopped for delivery to reduce bleeding risk. Prednisolone is not treatment for pre-eclampsia; corticosteroids in this context are for fetal lung maturity (betamethasone or dexamethasone). (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

Severe pre-eclampsia at 32+ weeks: acute BP control (IV labetalol 20 to 80 mg or IV hydralazine 5 to 10 mg), magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis, antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x2 24 hours apart) for fetal lung maturity as under 34 weeks, and planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours (after steroids complete) balancing maternal deterioration against preterm morbidity. Aspirin does not eliminate PET, only reduces incidence. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is fetal blood vessels running through membranes over the cervical os. A herald bleed with confirmed vasa praevia is an admission indication because membrane rupture causes fetal death within minutes from exsanguination. The plan is inpatient corticosteroids and planned caesarean at 34 to 35 weeks. Outpatient management or vaginal delivery is unsafe.
key_points: Confirmed vasa praevia plus any bleed equals admission until delivery
Elective caesarean at 34 to 35 weeks is standard timing after corticosteroids
Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in vasa praevia
Rescue steroids appropriate if prior course was more than 7 days ago and delivery anticipated within 7 days
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG recommends delivery at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks for confirmed vasa praevia; rescue betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart if last course over 7 days prior and delivery expected within 7 days.

options.rationale: Outpatient management after a sentinel bleed is unsafe because rupture of membranes causes fetal exsanguination in minutes; the woman must be in a facility able to expedite delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

Confirmed vasa praevia with a sentinel bleed at 32 weeks warrants inpatient admission until delivery, a rescue course of corticosteroids for lung maturity, and planned caesarean at 34 to 35 weeks to pre-empt catastrophic fetal exsanguination if membranes rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

The CTG is normal and the bleed is small and settled; immediate delivery at 32 weeks carries avoidable prematurity risk when planned delivery at 34 to 35 weeks after steroids is achievable. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

Vaginal delivery is absolutely contraindicated in confirmed vasa praevia because membrane rupture during labour causes catastrophic fetal haemorrhage from the exposed vessel. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is given peripartum in facility, not as home therapy, and cannot mitigate the acute exsanguination risk of vasa praevia with a herald bleed. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

explanation.summary: Early-onset severe FGR with absent UA end-diastolic flow but preserved DV a-wave and reactive CTG at 30 weeks is managed by inpatient surveillance. Delivery is triggered by DV a-wave becoming absent or reversed, spontaneous decelerations, computerised CTG short-term variation loss, or reaching 32 weeks. Delivery earlier than 32 weeks for UA changes alone increases prematurity morbidity without survival benefit.
key_points: UA absent EDF alone: inpatient surveillance until 32 weeks or DV decompensation
DV a-wave reversal or absence: deliver even before 32 weeks
Caesarean is the mode of choice for severe early-onset FGR
Magnesium neuroprotection given peripartum below 30 weeks (some centres 32)
explanation.pearls: TRUFFLE trial data: DV a-wave changes and computerised CTG STV are the triggers; before 32 weeks deliver on DV reversal, from 32 weeks deliver on UA absent EDF alone.

options.rationale: Outpatient monitoring is inadequate once UA end-diastolic flow is absent because deterioration to DV changes or CTG loss can occur within days; inpatient surveillance is required. (Source: RANZCOG Fetal Surveillance)

UA absent EDF alone without DV a-wave reversal or CTG decompensation does not mandate delivery before 32 weeks; premature intervention increases neonatal morbidity more than continued surveillance. (Source: RANZCOG Fetal Surveillance)

Isolated UA absent end-diastolic flow with a positive DV a-wave at 30 weeks allows brief inpatient surveillance because DV a-wave reversal or CTG abnormality is the accepted trigger for delivery before 32 weeks; empirical delivery now exposes to prematurity morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG Fetal Surveillance)

Induction is inappropriate because severe early-onset FGR tolerates labour poorly; if delivery is indicated, caesarean is safer. Rescue steroid decision is separate and does not itself mandate delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Fetal Surveillance)
Aspirin and heparin have no role in reversing established severe FGR; the intervention is surveillance and timely delivery, not late placental therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Fetal Surveillance)

explanation.summary: A deeply impacted head at caesarean in the second stage is a recognised obstetric emergency with maternal (uterine tears, bladder injury, PPH) and neonatal (hypoxia, skull fracture) risks. Reverse breech extraction, grasping a foot and delivering by breech extraction through the uterine incision, is faster and safer than repeated head disimpaction attempts. Vaginal push-up may work but should not be persisted with. Extending the uterine incision inferiorly risks bladder and cervical injury.
key_points: Reverse breech extraction is first-line for impacted head at caesarean
Do not extend uterine incision inferiorly (bladder and cervix at risk)
Upward J or T extension acceptable if more space needed
Avoid classical incision unless nothing else works
explanation.pearls: MODIFY trial (2024, UK) supports reverse breech extraction; RANZCOG endorses it as first-line manoeuvre. Prepare Patwardhan technique in advance for anticipated deep transverse arrest cases.

options.rationale: Tocolysis with terbutaline is not for impacted head at caesarean; it may add maternal tachycardia and delays definitive delivery when reverse breech extraction is available. (Source: RANZCOG Impacted Fetal Head)

Extending the uterine incision inferiorly risks bladder injury, extension into the cervix or vagina and heavy bleeding; upward J or T extension is the accepted rescue if space is needed, but reverse breech extraction should be attempted first. (Source: RANZCOG Impacted Fetal Head)
Vaginal push-up has already failed and prolongs delivery interval; continuing prolongs fetal hypoxia, and reverse breech extraction is faster and less injurious. (Source: RANZCOG Impacted Fetal Head)

Reverse breech extraction (Patwardhan or foot-first through the uterine incision) is the preferred manoeuvre for a deeply impacted head at caesarean because it avoids extending the uterine incision inferiorly and shortens delivery interval versus repeated failed head disimpaction. (Source: RANZCOG Impacted Fetal Head)

Classical incision commits the woman to caesarean in future pregnancies and carries higher morbidity; upward J extension is preferred if the lower incision is inadequate, and reverse breech extraction remains the first-line manoeuvre. (Source: RANZCOG Impacted Fetal Head)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is a clinical diagnosis of sudden cardiorespiratory collapse, hypoxia, seizure, and DIC in labour or early postpartum. Management is aggressive resuscitation with airway, breathing, circulation, blood products for coagulopathy, and perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes of cardiac arrest to improve maternal survival and enable resuscitation. Mortality remains high despite optimal care.
key_points: Triad: cardiorespiratory collapse, DIC, altered mental state or seizure in labour
Perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest
Early massive transfusion activation for DIC (FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets)
Vasopressors and inotropes for cardiovascular support; ECMO if available
explanation.pearls: SMFM AFE registry criteria: acute cardiorespiratory arrest or hypotension with respiratory compromise; DIC within 30 min; onset during labour or within 30 min of delivery; no fever above 38 C.

options.rationale: Delaying resuscitation for imaging in a periarrest woman is unsafe; bedside echocardiography may be done during resuscitation if it does not interrupt life-saving treatment. (Source: SOMANZ Obstetric Emergency)

Magnesium is for eclamptic seizures with hypertension and proteinuria; this presentation is anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy with shock and coagulopathy, requiring resuscitation and consideration of perimortem caesarean, not magnesium as first step. (Source: SOMANZ Obstetric Emergency)

Uterotonics and tranexamic acid may be part of PPH management but do not address the primary cardiorespiratory collapse of AFE; airway, breathing, circulation, and perimortem caesarean if in arrest take priority. (Source: SOMANZ Obstetric Emergency)

This is not anaphylaxis to a known trigger; it is amniotic fluid embolism, a distinct anaphylactoid syndrome. Adrenaline may be needed as an inotrope in cardiac arrest but IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis alone is inadequate. (Source: SOMANZ Obstetric Emergency)

The presentation is consistent with amniotic fluid embolism causing cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia, seizure and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy; management is resuscitation with perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes if cardiac arrest occurs, aggressive product replacement for coagulopathy, and inotropic and airway support. (Source: SOMANZ Obstetric Emergency)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is diagnosed on itch (often palms and soles) plus elevated serum bile acids. Severity is stratified by peak bile acids: mild (below 40), moderate (40 to 99), and severe (100 or greater). Severe ICP is associated with a substantially increased stillbirth risk that becomes marked from 36 weeks. Delivery timing is 35 to 36 weeks for severe ICP, 36 to 37 for moderate, and 37 to 38 for mild.
key_points: Bile acids 100 or more equals severe ICP; deliver at 35 to 36 weeks
Moderate ICP (40 to 99): deliver at 36 to 37 weeks
Mild ICP (10 to 39): deliver at 37 to 38 weeks
UDCA reduces itch but not stillbirth (PITCHES trial)
explanation.pearls: Ovadia meta-analysis (Lancet 2019): stillbirth risk rises steeply once peak bile acids reach 100 micromol/L, particularly beyond 36 weeks; ursodeoxycholic acid does not eliminate this risk.

options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid modestly reduces maternal itch but does not reduce stillbirth risk; continuing to 39 weeks in severe ICP with bile acids over 100 exposes the pregnancy to the stillbirth window. (Source: RANZCOG Intrahepatic Cholestasis)

Peak bile acids of 100 micromol/L or greater are associated with a significant stillbirth risk that increases at 36 weeks and beyond; RCOG and RANZCOG guidance is delivery at 35 to 36 weeks for severe intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Intrahepatic Cholestasis)

Immediate delivery today is not required; the excess stillbirth risk climbs sharply from 36 weeks onward, allowing time to plan induction and complete corticosteroid cover if needed before 34+6 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Intrahepatic Cholestasis)

Corticosteroids are not routinely indicated at 36+1 for lung maturity and expectant management to 38 weeks is not consistent with the elevated stillbirth risk of severe ICP. (Source: RANZCOG Intrahepatic Cholestasis)

Rifampicin is a second-line itch therapy in refractory cases and Doppler surveillance does not predict the acute stillbirth event in ICP; deferring delivery in severe ICP is not standard. (Source: RANZCOG Intrahepatic Cholestasis)

explanation.summary: Uterine inversion is a life-threatening obstetric emergency causing haemorrhage and neurogenic shock disproportionate to blood loss. Immediate treatment is bedside manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) with the placenta still attached, before uterotonics harden a constriction ring. Uterotonics and placental removal follow reduction. Failed manual reduction warrants theatre, tocolysis to relax the uterus, hydrostatic reduction, or surgical (Huntington or Haultain) procedures.
key_points: Immediate Johnson manoeuvre with placenta attached
Do NOT give uterotonics BEFORE reduction (creates constriction ring)
Do NOT remove placenta before reduction
Failed reduction: theatre with tocolysis (terbutaline or GA)
explanation.pearls: Neurogenic shock in inversion is out of proportion to blood loss (vagal traction on infundibulopelvic ligament); IV fluid resuscitation and atropine may be needed alongside reduction.

options.rationale: Rapid manual replacement of the fundus (Johnson manoeuvre) with the placenta still attached is the immediate first-line for uterine inversion; delay allows a constriction ring to form making replacement harder and haemorrhage worse. (Source: RANZCOG Uterine Inversion)

Removing the placenta before replacing the uterus dramatically worsens blood loss; the placenta acts as a partial haemostatic tamponade until reduction is achieved. (Source: RANZCOG Uterine Inversion)

Uterotonics before reduction cause a contraction ring that traps the inverted fundus and makes replacement impossible; uterotonics are used AFTER successful reduction. (Source: RANZCOG Uterine Inversion)
Balloon tamponade is not indicated in the inverted uterus and delays definitive reduction; balloons may be used after reduction if atony persists. (Source: RANZCOG Uterine Inversion)

Surgical reduction (Huntington or Haultain) is reserved for failed manual reduction; the first step is immediate bedside manual replacement, which succeeds in most cases. (Source: RANZCOG Uterine Inversion)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation to exclude endometrial cancer, which underlies roughly 10 percent of cases. Transvaginal ultrasound triages: thickness below 4 mm and homogenous has very low cancer risk; thickness 4 mm or more or heterogenous, focal, or vascular pattern requires tissue sampling. Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the reference standard because Pipelle sampling misses focal lesions.
key_points: PMB plus ET at or above 4 mm equals histology
Hysteroscopy plus directed biopsy is standard, superior to Pipelle for focal lesions
Risk factors: obesity, unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen, T2DM, PCOS, nulliparity, Lynch syndrome
Do not attribute PMB to atrophy without excluding malignancy
explanation.pearls: Endometrial thickness 4 mm is the RANZCOG cut-off (some international bodies use 5 mm). Persistent PMB with normal biopsy still warrants repeat sampling given up to 10% Pipelle miss rate.

options.rationale: Pipelle sampling alone can miss focal lesions and polyps; a negative Pipelle in the setting of thickened heterogenous endometrium still warrants hysteroscopy to exclude focal pathology. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Deferring histology in postmenopausal bleeding with endometrium above 4 mm risks missing endometrial cancer, which is present in roughly 10 percent of postmenopausal bleeding presentations. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness of 4 mm or greater requires histological sampling; hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the reference standard, particularly with heterogenous echo pattern that raises suspicion of endometrial cancer. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Attributing postmenopausal bleeding to atrophy without histological exclusion of malignancy is unsafe when the endometrial thickness is above 4 mm with a heterogenous pattern. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Staging imaging and tumour markers are for confirmed malignancy; histological diagnosis via hysteroscopy and biopsy must come first to justify any staging workup. (Source: RANZCOG Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI = U score x menopausal status x CA-125) triages adnexal masses. RMI above 200 identifies women at high risk of ovarian cancer who should have surgery in a specialist gynae-oncology centre because centralised care with complete staging improves survival. Percutaneous biopsy or generalist laparoscopy of a suspicious primary risks spillage and suboptimal staging.
key_points: RMI above 200 equals gynae-oncology referral
Postmenopausal, complex, solid or cystic mass with papillary projections raises suspicion
Do not biopsy a suspected ovarian primary percutaneously
Centralised surgery in specialist centres improves 5-year survival
explanation.pearls: RMI ultrasound score: 1 point each for multilocular, solid areas, bilateral, ascites, metastases (max 4). U=1 if 1 feature; U=3 if 2+ features. RMI = U x menopause (1 pre, 3 post) x CA-125.
