options.rationale: Delaying management in a postmenopausal complex mass with elevated CA-125 risks progression; there is no role for surveillance in a highly suspicious mass. (Source: eviQ Ovarian Cancer)

Percutaneous biopsy of a suspected ovarian primary risks tumour spillage and upstaging; diagnosis is by surgical excision with intraoperative frozen section in specialist centres. (Source: eviQ Ovarian Cancer)

Diagnostic laparoscopy outside a specialist centre in high-risk masses may complicate later staging and risks incomplete surgical cytoreduction; direct referral to a gynae-oncology unit is preferred. (Source: eviQ Ovarian Cancer)

Postmenopausal complex adnexal mass with elevated CA-125 and RMI above 200 has a high probability of ovarian malignancy; centralised surgery in a gynae-oncology centre with staging capability improves survival compared with generalist surgery. (Source: eviQ Ovarian Cancer)

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a valid option for advanced ovarian cancer but the decision is made by the gynae-oncology multidisciplinary team after diagnostic workup, not initiated in the referring service. (Source: eviQ Ovarian Cancer)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum with increta or percreta requires planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+0 weeks in a specialist centre with a multidisciplinary team on site. Attempted placental removal at caesarean is contraindicated because it triggers massive haemorrhage. Vaginal birth is contraindicated when placenta praevia coexists. Conservative in situ management is reserved for women wanting future fertility who accept the risks.
key_points: Suspected PAS with increta or percreta needs MDT delivery at 34 to 35 weeks
Do not attempt placental removal at caesarean when PAS is confirmed
Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in coexisting placenta praevia
In situ conservative management only when fertility preservation is wanted
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG recommends planned delivery at 34+0 to 35+0 weeks for suspected PAS; two units of packed red cells crossmatched with four on immediate standby, cell salvage available, and IR balloon occlusion catheters considered for percreta into bladder.

options.rationale: RANZCOG and international consensus recommend planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+0 weeks for suspected accreta spectrum, in a specialist centre with an MDT ready and blood on standby to minimise haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG PAS Guideline)

Waiting to 37 weeks in confirmed accreta risks an unplanned haemorrhage; attempted placental removal at delivery causes massive bleeding and is contraindicated in the increta or percreta setting. (Source: RANZCOG PAS Guideline)

Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in placenta praevia and accreta spectrum because cervical dilation over an adherent placenta produces uncontrolled haemorrhage requiring emergency laparotomy. (Source: RANZCOG PAS Guideline)

Leaving placenta in situ is a conservative option only for women who want future fertility and accept infection and delayed haemorrhage risk; it is not first line when the woman has completed her family. (Source: RANZCOG PAS Guideline)

A single small self-limited bleed with normal maternal and fetal status does not mandate immediate delivery; escalating to category-1 loses the benefit of planned MDT setup and additional steroid maturation. (Source: RANZCOG PAS Guideline)

explanation.summary: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome with recurrent early pregnancy loss is treated with low dose aspirin plus prophylactic low molecular weight heparin from confirmation of a viable pregnancy through to delivery and postnatally. Combination therapy improves live birth rates compared with aspirin alone. Therapeutic anticoagulation is reserved for prior VTE or catastrophic APS. Warfarin is contraindicated in early and late pregnancy.
key_points: Obstetric APS with recurrent early loss: aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH from viability
Aspirin alone is inferior to combination therapy for live birth
Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester and unsafe near term
Continue LMWH postnatally for 6 weeks as per standard prophylaxis rules
explanation.pearls: RCOG Green-top 17 defines obstetric APS as three or more consecutive losses under 10 weeks, one or more fetal deaths at or over 10 weeks, or one severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency before 34 weeks, plus persistent aPL antibodies 12 weeks apart; enoxaparin 40 mg daily is the standard prophylactic dose in booking weight under 90 kg.

options.rationale: Therapeutic anticoagulation is reserved for prior VTE or catastrophic APS, not for obstetric APS with recurrent early loss and no thrombosis history; hydroxychloroquine is not standard first line here. (Source: RCOG Green-top 17)
Aspirin alone is inferior to aspirin plus LMWH for live birth in obstetric APS with recurrent miscarriage; heparin is added regardless of VTE history in this indication. (Source: RCOG Green-top 17)

Obstetric APS with recurrent early pregnancy loss is treated with low dose aspirin plus prophylactic low molecular weight heparin from confirmation of pregnancy; combination therapy improves live birth rates over aspirin alone. (Source: RCOG Green-top 17)
Warfarin is teratogenic between 6 and 12 weeks and crosses the placenta at term causing fetal haemorrhage; it is contraindicated in obstetric APS in pregnancy. (Source: RCOG Green-top 17)
Corticosteroids do not improve live birth in obstetric APS and add gestational diabetes and preterm delivery risk; they are not part of first-line management. (Source: RCOG Green-top 17)

explanation.summary: Severe hypertension of 160/110 or above in pre-eclampsia requires rapid IV antihypertensive therapy with labetalol or hydralazine, alongside magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis, before or in parallel with delivery. Sublingual nifedipine is unsafe. Magnesium is superior to phenytoin. Furosemide is only for pulmonary oedema. Both mother and fetus benefit from timely blood pressure control and magnesium therapy before theatre.
key_points: Severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia is over 160 systolic or over 110 diastolic
IV labetalol 20 mg boluses or hydralazine 5 mg boluses are first line
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g per hour infusion for 24 hours postnatally
Do not use sublingual nifedipine because of unpredictable BP drops
explanation.pearls: SOMANZ target is BP under 160/110 within 30 to 60 minutes; magnesium toxicity signs are loss of patellar reflex then respiratory depression, reversed with calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL IV over 10 minutes.

options.rationale: Oral agents act too slowly for severe hypertension over 160/110 in the acute setting; IV agents and immediate magnesium prophylaxis are indicated before urgent delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

Uncontrolled severe hypertension at induction of general anaesthesia risks maternal stroke; blood pressure control and magnesium loading should be initiated before or in parallel with theatre transfer. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

Furosemide is not indicated in pre-eclampsia unless there is pulmonary oedema; sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated because of unpredictable severe blood pressure drops. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

Severe hypertension over 160/110 requires rapid IV antihypertensive therapy and concurrent magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis before delivery in severe pre-eclampsia; both are started immediately in parallel. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

Magnesium sulfate is superior to phenytoin for eclampsia prophylaxis and treatment; phenytoin has higher seizure recurrence and no maternal or perinatal benefit over magnesium. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe OHSS presents with haemoconcentration, ascites, oliguria, and dyspnoea after ovarian stimulation, worsened by ongoing pregnancy through endogenous hCG. Admission for careful IV crystalloid replacement, LMWH thromboprophylaxis, and paracentesis for symptomatic ascites is standard. Diuretics and elective surgery are contraindicated. Albumin has no proven benefit over crystalloid.
key_points: Severe OHSS features: HCT over 0.45, oliguria, ascites, dyspnoea, VTE risk
Admission plus IV crystalloid, LMWH prophylaxis, symptomatic paracentesis
Avoid diuretics, they worsen haemoconcentration and VTE risk
Surgery only for torsion, rupture, or ectopic pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Ongoing pregnancy prolongs and worsens OHSS through endogenous hCG; RANZCOG suggests LMWH prophylaxis for at least the duration of clinical OHSS and up to 12 weeks gestation in severe cases with haemoconcentration.

options.rationale: Albumin is not superior to crystalloid in OHSS and is not first line; oral fluid restriction worsens hypovolaemia and renal perfusion in an already haemoconcentrated patient. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Hyperstimulation Statement)

Ongoing pregnancy extends and worsens OHSS due to endogenous hCG; severe OHSS with haemoconcentration and dyspnoea requires admission not discharge. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Hyperstimulation Statement)

Diuretics worsen haemoconcentration and thrombosis risk in OHSS by removing intravascular volume; they are not first line. Withholding LMWH increases VTE risk further. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Hyperstimulation Statement)

Surgery on OHSS ovaries is reserved for torsion, rupture with haemorrhage, or ectopic pregnancy; ovaries are friable and elective decompression is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Hyperstimulation Statement)

Severe OHSS requires inpatient care with judicious volume expansion for haemoconcentration, LMWH thromboprophylaxis, and paracentesis for symptomatic ascites; targets are haematocrit under 0.45, urine output over 30 mL per hour, and symptom relief. (Source: RANZCOG Ovarian Hyperstimulation Statement)

explanation.summary: Retained placenta at 30 minutes with ongoing bleeding, or at 60 minutes without bleeding, is an indication for manual removal in theatre under regional or general anaesthetic with a concurrent oxytocin infusion. Sustained cord traction risks uterine inversion. Ergometrine may entrap the placenta. Balloon tamponade is used for atony after removal.
key_points: Retained placenta plus PPH at 30 minutes needs theatre manual removal
Give syntocinon 40 units in 500 mL crystalloid over 4 hours after removal
Ergometrine may cause placental entrapment and is avoided until placenta out
Prophylactic antibiotics at manual removal reduce endometritis
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG recommends a single dose IV cefazolin 2 g and metronidazole 500 mg at manual removal; risk of uterine inversion rises with sustained cord traction and fundal pressure without confirmed separation signs.

options.rationale: Retained placenta beyond 30 minutes with heavy ongoing bleeding needs prompt theatre transfer for manual removal under regional anaesthetic and an oxytocin infusion; delaying increases haemorrhage and infection risk. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

Ergometrine may worsen placental entrapment and does not remove a retained placenta; sustained cord traction without separation risks uterine inversion and cord avulsion. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)
Umbilical vein oxytocin has weak evidence and is not the standard next step when haemorrhage is ongoing; definitive management is manual removal in theatre. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)
Balloon tamponade is used after removal of the placenta for atonic bleeding; inserting a balloon over a retained placenta is not appropriate management. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)
Delaying beyond an hour with heavy ongoing bleeding is unsafe; timely manual removal reduces blood loss and morbidity in retained placenta with active haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: PPROM between 24 and 34 weeks is managed expectantly with inpatient surveillance, corticosteroids, and erythromycin, provided no infection or fetal compromise. Delivery is planned at 36 to 37 weeks or earlier for infection or non-reassuring CTG. Tocolysis is not indicated. Outpatient care is not standard. GBS chemoprophylaxis is added at delivery.
key_points: PPROM 24 to 34 weeks: expectant with steroids and erythromycin 250 mg 4 times daily 10 days
Deliver by 36 to 37 weeks, earlier for chorioamnionitis or fetal compromise
Tocolysis not indicated in PPROM without contractions
Inpatient care standard because of chorioamnionitis and cord accident risk
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG PPROM Statement recommends erythromycin 250 mg orally 4 times daily for 10 days; magnesium sulfate neuroprotection for anticipated preterm delivery under 30 weeks reduces cerebral palsy risk with number needed to treat around 60.

options.rationale: Expectant care beyond 34 weeks in PPROM increases chorioamnionitis and neonatal sepsis risk without meaningful neonatal benefit; planned delivery at 36 to 37 weeks is preferred with 34 as the earliest routine threshold in some guidelines. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)

Between 34 and 37 weeks, planned delivery is preferred over expectant care to reduce chorioamnionitis; RANZCOG suggests delivery by 36 to 37 weeks with earlier delivery for infection or fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)
At 32 weeks with no infection, prematurity risk still outweighs latency risk; delivery before 34 weeks is not indicated without infection or fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)
Outpatient management of PPROM is not standard in Australia because chorioamnionitis and cord accident risk requires inpatient CTG and observation. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)

Tocolysis is not indicated in PPROM without contractions and does not improve neonatal outcomes; a second steroid course is a rescue given only if delivery is anticipated in the next 7 days. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Statement)

explanation.summary: Rescue cervical cerclage between 16 and 27+6 weeks is offered for painless cervical dilation with prolapsed membranes in the absence of infection, ruptured membranes, contractions, or fetal compromise. It can prolong pregnancy by several weeks and improve neonatal survival. Progesterone treats a short cervix on ultrasound. Pessary evidence is weaker than cerclage for this indication.
key_points: Rescue cerclage: cervix dilated, membranes prolapsed, no infection or labour, 16 to 27+6 weeks
Vaginal progesterone is for short cervix on scan, not dilated cervix
Absolute contraindications: infection, ruptured membranes, active labour, fetal compromise
Counsel about risks of infection and iatrogenic membrane rupture
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG cites rescue cerclage prolonging gestation by around 4 to 6 weeks on average and increasing 34-week delivery from around 20 to over 60 percent; McDonald technique is standard, avoid Shirodkar in the emergency setting.

sources.label: NICE Preterm Labour and Birth NG25

options.rationale: 22+3 weeks is periviability and expectant management with rescue cerclage in the absence of infection can extend gestation meaningfully; immediate delivery discards potential viability. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

Vaginal progesterone is for short cervix on ultrasound, not for dilated cervix with prolapsed membranes; rescue cerclage is a valid option in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

Rescue cerclage between 16 and 27+6 weeks with dilated cervix and no infection or contractions can prolong pregnancy and improve neonatal survival; NICE and RANZCOG support offering it after counselling. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

Pessary evidence is mixed and inferior to cerclage in dilated cervix with prolapsed membranes; outpatient management at this stage is unsafe due to imminent labour risk. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

Prolapsed membranes without rupture are not an absolute contraindication to rescue cerclage; refusing cerclage on that basis alone forgoes the intervention with best chance to prolong pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Insufficiency Statement)

explanation.summary: Painless antepartum haemorrhage in the third trimester requires placenta praevia to be excluded before any digital vaginal examination. Transabdominal ultrasound with transvaginal follow-up is safe and defines placental edge relative to the internal os. If praevia is confirmed at 32 weeks, admit, give a course of antenatal corticosteroids, cross-match blood, and plan elective caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks unless bleeding forces earlier delivery. Screen for placenta accreta spectrum in women with prior caesarean.
key_points: Painless APH: exclude praevia before digital examination
TAUS then TVUS is safe and accurate
Steroids for lung maturity 24 to less than 34 weeks
Anti-D if Rh D negative; Kleihauer to quantify large FMH
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG lower placental edge threshold for praevia is any placental tissue within 2 cm of the internal os on TVUS in the third trimester; edges 2-5 cm from os are termed low-lying and may allow vaginal birth after individualised review.

options.rationale: Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated until placenta praevia has been excluded by ultrasound because it can precipitate torrential haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

There is no indication for expedited delivery in a haemodynamically stable mother with reassuring CTG at 32 weeks before the placental site is defined; oxytocin risks massive haemorrhage if praevia. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

Painless antepartum haemorrhage with a documented low placenta at 20 weeks and no repeat scan must be evaluated with ultrasound; transabdominal then transvaginal is safe with a well-defined technique and defines placenta praevia or accreta prior to any speculum or digital examination. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

The mother is Rh D positive, so anti-D is not indicated; Kleihauer is used in Rh D negative women or for suspected large feto-maternal haemorrhage volume estimation, not first-line here. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

Even a small antepartum haemorrhage from suspected praevia can herald a larger sentinel bleed; admission for further imaging, steroids if praevia confirmed, and observation is standard. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia Statement)

explanation.summary: Australian gestational diabetes diagnosis follows ADIPS 75 g OGTT thresholds: fasting 5.1 mmol/L or higher, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or higher, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or higher (any one). Management starts with dietitian-led carbohydrate distribution and glucose monitoring four times daily. Targets are fasting under 5.0, 1 hour postprandial under 7.4, or 2 hour under 6.7. Pharmacotherapy is added if targets are not met after 1 to 2 weeks or if fetal macrosomia develops. Metformin and insulin are both first-line pharmacotherapy in Australian practice.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds diagnose GDM on any one abnormal value
Diet plus SMBG four times daily is first-line
Metformin or insulin added if fasting >=5.0 or 1 hour >=7.4
Universal 75 g OGTT screening at 24 to 28 weeks in AU
explanation.pearls: ADIPS uses a lower fasting cut-off than the WHO 1999 criteria (5.1 vs 7.0 mmol/L), yielding higher diagnostic rates; treatment reduces macrosomia and shoulder dystocia but effect on caesarean rate is modest.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

options.rationale: Fasting 5.4 mmol/L and 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L both exceed ADIPS 75 g OGTT thresholds for GDM; the diagnosis is made and further management is required. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

ADIPS thresholds (fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5) diagnose GDM if any one is met or exceeded; first-line management is dietary modification with SMBG four times daily (fasting plus 1 or 2 hour postprandial), progressing to metformin or insulin if targets not met. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

First-line is diet and exercise with SMBG; pharmacotherapy is added when 1 to 2 weeks of dietary modification fails to achieve fasting <5.0 and 1 hour postprandial <7.4 (or 2 hour <6.7). (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

Insulin is added when dietary measures fail targets; jumping to insulin before a trial of diet plus SMBG is not the AU pathway even with risk factors for macrosomia. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)
A single OGTT meeting ADIPS thresholds diagnoses GDM; repeating the OGTT delays management and is not indicated. (Source: ADIPS GDM Diagnostic Criteria 2014)

explanation.summary: Primary postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony is managed with a stepwise combination of resuscitation and uterotonics. First-line is oxytocin (10 units IM or IV bolus plus infusion). Second-line depends on comorbidity: ergometrine 250 mcg IM/IV is avoided in hypertension and pre-eclampsia; carboprost 250 mcg IM is the alternative and repeatable to 2 mg total; misoprostol 800 mcg sublingual is an adjunct where injectables are limited. IV tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours reduces bleeding-related mortality (WOMAN trial). Failure to control bleeding prompts intrauterine balloon tamponade, then brace sutures, uterine artery ligation or embolisation, and hysterectomy as last resort.
key_points: Oxytocin first, then carboprost if ergometrine contraindicated
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours in all cases
Escalate to tamponade, brace suture, embolisation, hysterectomy
Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia
explanation.pearls: Carboprost is a synthetic 15-methyl PGF2 alpha; contraindicated in active asthma because of bronchospasm risk; requires refrigeration; peak effect within 20 minutes.

options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive disease because of severe hypertensive crisis risk; the RANZCOG PPH pathway skips ergometrine and moves to carboprost in hypertension. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

Balloon tamponade is an important step once uterotonics have failed but comes after the second uterotonic escalation; it is not the first response to persistent atony while carboprost remains an option. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

With ergometrine relatively contraindicated in hypertension, next-line is IM carboprost 250 mcg (repeatable every 15 min to 2 mg total) plus IV tranexamic acid 1 g given within 3 hours; TXA reduces mortality per WOMAN trial. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

Misoprostol is used where injectable agents unavailable or as adjunct; carboprost is more potent and preferred where available with an IV in place, particularly with hypertension precluding ergometrine. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

Hysterectomy is the last resort after failed uterotonics, tamponade, brace suture, and interventional radiology; a second uterotonic and TXA are earlier steps in the escalation pathway. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: Clinical chorioamnionitis is diagnosed by maternal fever plus at least two of maternal tachycardia, fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor, and maternal leukocytosis. Management is IV broad spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin plus gentamicin, adding metronidazole or clindamycin for anaerobic cover post-caesarean) and expedited delivery regardless of gestation because expectant management increases neonatal sepsis, cerebral palsy, and maternal septic shock. Tocolysis is contraindicated. Vaginal birth is preferred unless obstetric indications require caesarean.
key_points: Fever plus two of: mat/fetal tachycardia, tender uterus, offensive liquor, leukocytosis
IV amp + gentamicin + metronidazole is typical AU regimen
Expedite delivery; do not tocolyse
Neonatal team standby for early onset sepsis
explanation.pearls: The ORACLE II arm found erythromycin (not amoxicillin with clavulanic acid) reduces neonatal composite morbidity in PPROM without chorioamnionitis; amoxicillin with clavulanic acid in PPROM increased necrotising enterocolitis so amoxicillin plus clavulanate is avoided in this setting.

sources.label: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.rationale: Fever, tachycardia (maternal and fetal), raised inflammatory markers, uterine tenderness, and offensive liquor meet clinical chorioamnionitis criteria; oral macrolide alone is inadequate and delaying delivery risks maternal sepsis and fetal death. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.rationale: Clinical chorioamnionitis mandates IV broad spectrum antibiotics (typical AU regimen ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole) and expedited delivery irrespective of gestation because ongoing infection worsens neonatal and maternal outcomes; neonatal team standby is essential at 30 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in chorioamnionitis; a second course of steroids is not appropriate when the priority is delivery to reduce maternal and fetal harm from ongoing sepsis. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.rationale: Amniocentesis in overt clinical chorioamnionitis delays definitive management; clinical criteria are sufficient to start antibiotics and expedite delivery without waiting for culture. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

options.rationale: Discharge with oral antibiotics is unsafe in overt chorioamnionitis; the patient requires IV antibiotics and delivery in a facility with neonatal intensive care support. (Source: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG Preterm Prelabour Rupture of Membranes Statement

explanation.summary: Superimposed pre-eclampsia on chronic hypertension or chronic kidney disease is diagnosed when new severe hypertension emerges after 20 weeks with new organ dysfunction (thrombocytopenia under 150, creatinine above baseline, ALT/AST above 2x normal, cerebral or visual symptoms, pulmonary oedema) or a doubling of the baseline proteinuria plus new organ dysfunction. Severe features mandate admission, BP control with oral nifedipine IR, IV labetalol, or IV hydralazine, IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis (4 g loading dose over 20 min then 1 g per hour), and timely delivery. Antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity are appropriate 24 to less than 34 weeks.
key_points: Superimposed pre-eclampsia: new organ dysfunction on chronic HTN/CKD
Treat severe HTN: nifedipine IR, labetalol IV, hydralazine IV
MgSO4 4 g load then 1 g/h for seizure prophylaxis
ACE inhibitors and ARBs contraindicated in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: MgSO4 toxicity signs: loss of patellar reflex (first), respiratory depression, then cardiac; calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent solution IV is the antidote; monitor reflexes, respirations, and urine output rather than levels in most units.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guidelines Hypertension in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Steroids are appropriate but deferring delivery to 37 weeks with severe features (visual symptoms, thrombocytopenia, LFT derangement, growth restriction) risks eclampsia, HELLP progression, and placental abruption; delivery is timely after stabilisation, typically within 24-48 hours. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetotoxicity (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios); outpatient management is unsafe with severe features. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Prazosin is a second or third-line antihypertensive in pregnancy; severe pre-eclampsia with cerebral symptoms needs immediate parenteral or oral rapid-acting therapy (labetalol IV or nifedipine IR) and admission, not outpatient escalation. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Discharging severe hypertension with cerebral symptoms and fetal growth restriction is unsafe; the risk of eclampsia, stroke, and placental abruption mandates admission. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

Severe hypertension with cerebral symptoms, thrombocytopenia trend, rising creatinine above baseline, raised ALT, fetal growth restriction, and proteinuria more than doubled from baseline meets superimposed pre-eclampsia with severe features; treatment is BP control (labetalol or nifedipine IR), magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/h, and delivery. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia describes unprotected fetal vessels traversing the membranes near the internal os, unsupported by cord or placental tissue. Risk factors include velamentous cord insertion, low-lying or bilobed placenta, and multiple pregnancy from IVF. Antenatal diagnosis by TVUS with colour Doppler allows planned elective caesarean at 35-36 weeks. Undiagnosed vasa praevia presents with bleeding at rupture of membranes and rapid fetal decompensation (sinusoidal CTG or bradycardia) because fetal blood volume is around 250-300 mL; delivery must occur within minutes. Category 1 caesarean is life-saving; general anaesthesia is often quickest.
key_points: Velamentous cord and low placenta are the main risks
Antenatally diagnosed: planned CS at 35-36 weeks
Bleeding at ARM plus sinusoidal CTG: immediate CS
Fetal survival depends on delivery within minutes
explanation.pearls: Sinusoidal CTG has a smooth undulating baseline of 5-15 bpm amplitude with 3-5 cycles/min for at least 20 minutes and no accelerations; it reflects severe fetal anaemia (haemorrhage, alloimmunisation, feto-maternal haemorrhage).

options.rationale: The bleeding is fetal, not maternal; tranexamic acid does not treat fetal blood loss and delays definitive delivery which is the only intervention that saves the fetus. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

Intrauterine resuscitation is appropriate for hypertonic decelerations but sinusoidal pattern with maternal bleeding at ARM signals fetal exsanguination; delay of 15 minutes risks fetal death, not category 1 caesarean is required. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

Apt or Kleihauer testing is diagnostically supportive but takes time; sinusoidal CTG with bleeding at ARM in a known velamentous insertion is treated as vasa praevia and delivered immediately. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

Ultrasound confirms vasa praevia prospectively but is not the correct step during acute rupture with fetal compromise; the diagnostic pathway is clinical and delivery is immediate. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

Vaginal bleeding at rupture of membranes with sinusoidal CTG in a woman with velamentous cord insertion is vasa praevia rupture with fetal exsanguination; category 1 caesarean under general anaesthesia (fastest to delivery) with paediatric team standby is life-saving. (Source: RANZCOG Vasa Praevia Statement)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum in the presence of prior caesareans plus placenta praevia is a high-risk situation for massive haemorrhage; hysterectomy is often the definitive treatment when conservative approaches fail. In a Jehovah's Witness with a valid advance directive refusing donor blood products, the patient's autonomy must be respected and management planned around blood conservation. Accepted strategies include intraoperative cell salvage, IV tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours, meticulous surgical haemostasis, recombinant factor concentrates, and early hysterectomy rather than protracted conservative attempts. Uterine artery embolisation and internal iliac ligation are alternatives where accessible. Discussion of the advance directive should occur antenatally and be re-documented.
key_points: PAS spectrum needs multidisciplinary planning antenatally
Respect valid advance directive: no donor blood
Cell salvage plus TXA plus early hysterectomy is the pathway
Recombinant factor VIIa is salvage adjunct, not first-line
explanation.pearls: Cell salvage in obstetrics is safe when a leukocyte depletion filter is used to remove amniotic fluid contaminants; anti-D is required for Rh D negative women receiving Rh D positive salvaged blood, and the volume returned can be dose-guided by Kleihauer testing.

options.rationale: Waiting 10 minutes with ongoing 1.8 L loss in a patient who refuses transfusion is unsafe; cell salvage should be activated immediately along with IV TXA 1 g and mechanical control (uterine compression, aortic compression, balloon) plus preparation for hysterectomy. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

Balloon tamponade is an option but relying on it alone with ongoing torrential bleeding from placenta accreta in a patient refusing blood is inadequate; cell salvage, TXA, aortic compression, and prompt hysterectomy planning are required. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

The patient has an explicit written advance directive refusing donor blood products; overriding a competent adult's directive is unlawful and unethical, even in emergency. (Source: NHMRC Advance Care Planning)

Refractory PPH with atony and adherent placenta with 1.8 L loss in a patient refusing donor blood requires simultaneous cell salvage activation, IV TXA 1 g, mechanical control (bimanual and aortic compression, balloon), and immediate progression to hysterectomy given placenta accreta spectrum and patient's advance directive limiting bridging measures. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

Recombinant factor VIIa is a salvage adjunct when fibrinogen and platelets are adequate and bleeding persists; it is not first-line before mechanical control, TXA, and cell salvage. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Statement)

explanation.summary: Australia uses risk-based and universal-screening GBS prophylaxis policies depending on jurisdiction; where universal screening is done, the swab is collected at 35-37 weeks. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g four-hourly until birth. Adequate prophylaxis is at least 4 hours before birth, though any exposure confers some benefit. For non-anaphylaxis penicillin allergy, IV cefazolin 2 g then 1 g eight-hourly. For anaphylaxis-risk penicillin allergy with unknown susceptibility, IV vancomycin or clindamycin (if susceptible). Term PROM with GBS colonisation is an indication for immediate antibiotic commencement and induction rather than prolonged expectancy.
key_points: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g Q4H until birth
GBS-positive term PROM = antibiotics + induction
Adequate prophylaxis is ≥4 hours pre-birth
Non-anaphylaxis allergy: cefazolin; anaphylaxis: vancomycin/clindamycin
GBS colonisation alone is not an indication for caesarean
explanation.pearls: Late preterm PROM (34-36+6 weeks) with GBS-positive status also warrants immediate benzylpenicillin plus induction unless steroids are indicated; delaying birth in preterm PROM is a distinct decision balanced against pulmonary maturity.

options.rationale: GBS-positive women receive intrapartum antibiotics from the time of PROM at term, not only in established labour. Expectant management beyond 24 hours in a GBS-positive woman substantially increases neonatal early-onset GBS sepsis risk. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS)

RANZCOG intrapartum GBS guidance recommends IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g four-hourly for all women with GBS colonisation at any point of labour (or ruptured membranes) at term. Induction of labour is offered from the outset for term PROM to reduce chorioamnionitis and neonatal infection risk. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS)

Oral amoxicillin achieves inadequate intra-amniotic concentrations; intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is IV, not oral. Delaying by hours in a GBS-positive PROM woman is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS)

GBS colonisation alone is not an indication for caesarean. Antibiotic prophylaxis during vaginal birth is standard care and reduces early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis to below 0.5 per 1000 births. Caesarean carries substantially higher maternal morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS)

Adequate GBS prophylaxis requires a loading dose followed by regular dosing until birth (penicillin four-hourly, cefazolin eight-hourly). A single dose is inadequate. Cefazolin is reserved for low-anaphylaxis-risk penicillin allergy. (Source: RANZCOG intrapartum GBS)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG criteria for methotrexate in tubal ectopic pregnancy are: haemodynamically stable, no fetal cardiac activity, unruptured, adnexal mass under 3.5 cm, bhCG under 5000 IU/L, no significant pain, minimal free fluid, no contraindications (normal renal, hepatic, haematological function; not breastfeeding; no folate supplements or immunosuppression; no active peptic ulcer), and reliable follow-up. The single-dose regimen is 50 mg/m2 IM, with bhCG day 0, day 4 and day 7. If bhCG has fallen ≥15 percent between day 4 and 7, weekly bhCG to undetectable. If not, second dose. Persistent trophoblast rates require weekly bhCG to zero over ~4 to 8 weeks. Give anti-D 250 IU IM if rhesus negative.
key_points: MTX criteria: stable, no FCA, <3.5 cm, bhCG <5000, no pain/fluid/contraindications, reliable follow-up
Single-dose 50 mg/m2 IM, day 4 and day 7 bhCG
≥15% fall day 4-7 = weekly bhCG to zero; <15% = second dose
Surgical management for bhCG ≥5000 IU/L or fetal cardiac activity
Give anti-D if rhesus negative and bleeding or MTX given
explanation.pearls: A woman treated with methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy should avoid conception for at least 3 months due to teratogenic risk and take a folate-free multivitamin during that interval; folate rescues methotrexate and reduces efficacy in the acute treatment window.

options.rationale: Expectant management is appropriate for very low bhCG (usually under 1000 IU/L) with a falling trend, minimal symptoms, no visible mass or trophoblast on scan. bhCG of 3400 with a visible 2.2 cm adnexal mass exceeds this threshold. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

Salpingectomy is indicated for haemodynamic instability, mass over 3.5 cm, bhCG over 5000 IU/L, fetal cardiac activity or failed methotrexate. This patient meets criteria for medical management which is safer and preserves the tube. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

RANZCOG methotrexate criteria: stable patient, no fetal cardiac activity, mass under 3.5 cm, bhCG under 5000 IU/L, no significant pain, no significant free fluid, no contraindications (normal renal, hepatic, haematological function, not breastfeeding, no folate replacement), reliable follow-up. This patient meets every criterion. Single-dose regimen is standard AU practice, with bhCG measured pre-treatment, day 4 (peak) and day 7 (expected 15 percent fall), then weekly to undetectable. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

Australian standard practice is a single-dose regimen with success rate around 88 percent for bhCG under 5000. A second dose is given if bhCG has not fallen by 15 percent between days 4 and 7. Routine day-0-and-day-4 dosing is a different (multi-dose) protocol used less commonly. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)
Direct intralesional methotrexate is not standard AU practice and offers no advantage over systemic IM administration in eligible patients with tubal ectopic. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia is defined by BP ≥160/110 or by any milder BP with severe features (persistent neurological symptoms, epigastric pain with hepatic tenderness, low platelets, hepatic transaminase elevation, renal impairment, pulmonary oedema, or fetal compromise). Management is parallel BP control (IV labetalol 20-80 mg or hydralazine 5-10 mg, or oral nifedipine 10-20 mg immediate release), eclampsia prophylaxis with magnesium sulfate (4 g IV over 20 min then 1 g/hr, 24 hours post-birth or last seizure), and expedited birth at ≥37 weeks. Fluid balance is meticulous - total fluids restricted to 80 mL/hr and total input under 2500 mL/24 hr - because pulmonary oedema kills.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia = BP ≥160/110 OR severe features
IV labetalol/hydralazine + magnesium sulfate + expedited birth ≥37/40
Magnesium: 4 g load over 20 min then 1 g/hr, continue 24 hr post-birth
Fluids restricted (~80 mL/hr max, <2500 mL/24 hr) to prevent pulmonary oedema
Do not use furosemide for BP control - only for pulmonary oedema
explanation.pearls: Magnesium toxicity monitoring: loss of patellar reflex (~4 mmol/L), respiratory depression (~5 mmol/L), cardiac arrest (~7 mmol/L); antidote is 1 g IV calcium gluconate slow injection.

options.rationale: Oral methyldopa is a maintenance agent for mild to moderate hypertension with slow onset (2-4 hours). Severe pre-eclampsia with BP ≥160/110 requires IV control within minutes to reduce stroke risk; oral first-line here is unsafe. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

Severe pre-eclampsia at term with signs of severe features (BP ≥160/110, symptoms, hyperreflexia with clonus, biochemical abnormality, fetal compromise) demands immediate parallel control of BP and eclampsia prophylaxis. IV labetalol 20 mg (then 40 mg, then 80 mg every 10 min to max 220 mg) or hydralazine 5 mg is the first-line antihypertensive; magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hr is the eclampsia prophylaxis. At 37 weeks with severe features, expedited birth is indicated. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

Sublingual nifedipine causes uncontrolled BP drop and is not standard; oral immediate-release nifedipine (not sublingual) is a valid option. Magnesium is given in parallel, not delayed - drug interaction is manageable clinically. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

Pre-eclamptic women are intravascularly depleted despite oedema. Furosemide worsens uteroplacental perfusion and is only indicated for confirmed pulmonary oedema, never for BP control in pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

Magnesium sulfate is superior to diazepam and phenytoin for eclampsia prophylaxis and treatment (MAGPIE and Eclampsia Trial). Diazepam is not standard AU therapy. BP still needs treating. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a severe form of pre-eclampsia occurring in around 10 to 20 percent of severe pre-eclampsia cases. Diagnostic thresholds (Mississippi/Tennessee) include LDH >600 U/L or bilirubin >20 micromol/L with schistocytes, AST/ALT >70 U/L, and platelets <100 x10^9/L. Delivery is definitive. Beyond 34 weeks, deliver within 24-48 hours after stabilisation. Between 24 and 34 weeks, if maternal and fetal condition permit, give 48 hours of corticosteroids before delivery; if unstable, deliver sooner. Magnesium sulfate is used for eclampsia prophylaxis and continued for 24 hours postpartum. Complications include hepatic haematoma or rupture, DIC, acute kidney injury and abruption.
key_points: HELLP: LDH >600, AST/ALT >70, platelets <100 with schistocytes
Beyond 34/40 - deliver within 24-48 hours after stabilisation
Magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis (24 hr postpartum)
Route by cervical favourability and fetal status - not automatic caesarean
Watch for hepatic rupture, DIC, AKI, abruption
explanation.pearls: Persistent HELLP over 72 hours postpartum should prompt consideration of thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes (aHUS, TTP, pregnancy-associated TMA), which require ADAMTS13 testing and complement studies plus a haematology consult.

options.rationale: In HELLP with worsening features, delivery should not routinely be delayed 48 hours for antenatal corticosteroids because maternal deterioration risk (hepatic haematoma rupture, DIC, eclampsia) is high. If a short window is safe (12-24 hours) and clinical picture is stable, a single dose may be given while planning birth, but full 48 hour delay is not appropriate. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

Prophylactic platelet transfusion in HELLP is not indicated except for active bleeding or preparation for surgery/regional anaesthesia in a patient at <50 x10^9/L. Delaying delivery based on the platelet count worsens outcomes because HELLP typically continues to progress until birth. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

HELLP is a life-threatening variant of severe pre-eclampsia with maternal mortality up to 4 percent; expectant outpatient management is contraindicated. Delivery is definitive; delay increases hepatic rupture, DIC and eclampsia risk. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

Category-1 caesarean is reserved for immediate threat to maternal or fetal life. Here, the mother is stable and the fetus is reassuring; delivery within 24-48 hours after stabilisation is safer than crash surgery in a coagulopathic patient. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

This is HELLP syndrome (haemolysis with schistocytes, LDH >600, elevated liver enzymes >70, platelets <100). At 34+5 with stable maternal status but worsening laboratory features, admit, start magnesium for eclampsia prophylaxis, give one antenatal corticosteroid dose, and plan birth within 24-48 hours. Route of delivery is guided by cervical favourability and fetal status. Multidisciplinary involvement (obstetrics, anaesthetics, haematology, neonatology) is essential. (Source: SOMANZ pre-eclampsia)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is declared when routine axial traction fails to deliver the shoulders after birth of the head. The RANZCOG HELPERR sequence is: Help (call), Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic - downward and lateral), Enter (internal rotational manoeuvres - Rubin II or Woods screw), Remove posterior arm, Roll (Gaskin all-fours). Each step is given 30 seconds before escalating. Force is not the answer - do not apply excessive traction, do not apply fundal pressure. Cleidotomy, symphysiotomy or Zavanelli manoeuvre are last resort. Team communication and clear time-stamped documentation are essential.
key_points: HELPERR: Help, Evaluate episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal), Remove posterior arm, Roll (Gaskin)
Never apply fundal pressure - worsens impaction
Only routine axial traction - excessive traction causes brachial plexus injury
30 seconds per manoeuvre before escalating
Time-stamped documentation and post-event debrief mandatory
explanation.pearls: The posterior arm delivery (Menticoglou manoeuvre) has the highest success rate of the internal manoeuvres and should be the primary internal step when first-line external manoeuvres fail in most contemporary AU teaching.

options.rationale: McRoberts is correct but fundal pressure is absolutely contraindicated - it worsens shoulder impaction and increases the risk of uterine rupture and neonatal injury. Suprapubic pressure is the correct adjunct. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)
Zavanelli is a last-resort rescue after failed internal manoeuvres, associated with high fetal and maternal morbidity. It is never the first response. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

Increased downward traction on the head is the direct cause of brachial plexus (Erb's palsy) and clavicular injury in shoulder dystocia. Routine axial traction only is applied; force is never the answer. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

Cleidotomy is a last-resort manoeuvre used only when all first- and second-line approaches have failed and there is no other route. Attempting fracture as first-line is inappropriate and unnecessarily traumatic. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

The Australian HELPERR/RANZCOG sequence starts with McRoberts (hyperflexion of hips to flatten the sacrum and rotate the pubic symphysis cephalad) plus suprapubic pressure directed downwards and laterally to dislodge the anterior shoulder from behind the pubis. Only routine axial traction is applied; excessive downward traction risks brachial plexus injury. If unsuccessful within 30 seconds, proceed to internal manoeuvres. (Source: RANZCOG shoulder dystocia)

explanation.summary: PPROM before 24 weeks carries very poor prognosis - counsel about the futility threshold with neonatology involvement. Between 24 and 34 weeks, expectant inpatient management is standard, with latency antibiotics (erythromycin, 10 days), antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone), and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection where delivery is likely within 24 hours (under 30 weeks in Australian guidance). Continuous surveillance for chorioamnionitis (temperature, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia, rising inflammatory markers, purulent discharge) mandates expedited birth. Tocolysis is not standard. Beyond 34 weeks, expectant management for GBS-negative women is reasonable to 37 weeks; GBS-positive women deliver at 34-36 weeks.
key_points: Erythromycin (NOT amoxicillin with clavulanic acid - NEC risk) for 10 days latency
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x 2 (24 hr apart) or dexamethasone 6 mg IM x 4 (12 hr apart)
Magnesium sulfate neuroprotection <30 weeks when delivery imminent
Inpatient surveillance for chorioamnionitis; deliver if infection develops
Tocolysis is not standard in PPROM
explanation.pearls: For PPROM approaching 34 weeks, the PPROMT trial supports expectant management to 37 weeks in GBS-negative women without infection, but jurisdictional practice varies; GBS-positive PPROM at 34 weeks typically triggers delivery with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.

options.rationale: Expectant management is offered at 24+3 without evidence of infection or fetal compromise, with continuous surveillance for chorioamnionitis and fetal wellbeing. Immediate delivery of a 610 g fetus has extremely poor outcomes without the benefit of corticosteroids or magnesium. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is contraindicated in PPROM because of the necrotising enterocolitis signal from the ORACLE I trial - erythromycin is the correct AU choice. Magnesium neuroprotection is offered under 30 weeks per AU guidance and is a critical omission here. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

Tocolysis has no proven benefit in PPROM (it may prolong latency briefly but does not improve neonatal outcome) and can mask chorioamnionitis. Latency antibiotics improve neonatal outcomes and are not withheld until infection is manifest. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

PPROM at 24+3 without infection warrants latency antibiotics (erythromycin - not amoxicillin with clavulanic acid which increases necrotising enterocolitis risk per ORACLE trial), antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart), and magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection where delivery is anticipated within 24 hours before 30 weeks (Australian NNS/AAGBI recommendation extends to 30 weeks with MAGENTA data). Neonatology counsels the mother about survival and morbidity at extreme preterm gestation. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

PPROM at extreme preterm gestation warrants inpatient admission for daily observation of temperature, uterine tenderness, CTG and inflammatory markers, and readiness to expedite birth for chorioamnionitis. Outpatient management is not standard AU practice. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM)

explanation.summary: The decision between salpingotomy and salpingectomy in tubal ectopic pregnancy hinges on the state of the contralateral tube. If the contralateral tube is healthy, salpingotomy preserves natural fertility potential and is preferred if surgeon-appropriate. If the contralateral tube is absent or diseased, contemporary evidence favours salpingectomy of the affected tube: the recurrent-ectopic risk in a damaged residual tube is high, persistent trophoblast complicates salpingotomy in 5-15 percent, and IVF bypasses tubal factors entirely with acceptable success. This inverts the intuitive 'preserve the tube' response. Preoperative counselling should explicitly discuss the IVF pathway.
key_points: Salpingotomy = preserved contralateral tube; salpingectomy = absent/damaged contralateral tube
Salpingotomy carries 5-15% persistent trophoblast + 15-20% recurrent ectopic in same tube
IVF bypasses tubal factor entirely - acceptable path to conception
Fetal cardiac activity, bhCG >5000, haemoperitoneum = surgery, not methotrexate
Counsel about IVF preoperatively when salpingectomy is planned
explanation.pearls: In tubal ectopic managed by salpingotomy, weekly bhCG monitoring to undetectable is mandatory - persistent trophoblast requires additional single-dose methotrexate or repeat surgery if bhCG plateaus above 5 IU/L.

options.rationale: In a woman with a prior contralateral salpingectomy, the remaining tube is her only conduit for spontaneous conception, but the risk of recurrent ectopic in the SAME tube after salpingotomy is 15-20 percent, plus persistent trophoblast requiring further treatment. Contemporary RANZCOG and international consensus favour salpingectomy in this specific scenario because ART (IVF) bypasses the tube entirely and salpingotomy leaves a damaged residual tube that dominates recurrence risk. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

Methotrexate is contraindicated - fetal cardiac activity is present, bhCG exceeds 5000 IU/L, there is significant haemoperitoneum and haemodynamic instability. Immediate operative management is mandatory. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

In a woman with prior contralateral salpingectomy, salpingectomy of the affected tube is preferred over salpingotomy because the recurrent-ectopic risk in the same (damaged) tube outweighs the loss of tubal fertility, and IVF bypasses the tubal factor entirely. This trickiness pattern (T14 historical bilaterality flip) inverts the standard 'preserve the tube' teaching. Counsel about IVF pathways preoperatively. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

Oophorectomy is not indicated in tubal ectopic pregnancy. Laparotomy versus laparoscopy is a decision based on stability and surgeon skill; laparoscopy is preferred if stable and appropriately equipped. Preserving the ovary is important for future ART cycles. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

Direct intralesional methotrexate is not standard practice and is contraindicated in unstable patients with active bleeding. Surgery is mandatory given haemoperitoneum, fetal cardiac activity, and haemodynamic compromise. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG PPH management follows a stepwise algorithm: uterotonics, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, examination for genital tract trauma or retained products, bimanual compression and intrauterine balloon, uterine artery ligation and B-Lynch or similar compression suture, then uterine artery embolisation (if stable and transfer feasible) or peripartum hysterectomy. Each step is time-critical - PPH deaths cluster in the second hour of bleeding, and delay in progressing to definitive surgery is a modifiable mortality determinant. UAE is fertility-preserving but requires haemodynamic stability. Hysterectomy is the definitive intervention when the patient is exsanguinating, coagulopathic, and already in theatre - fertility conversations, however important, do not override the immediate need for survival.
key_points: PPH pathway: uterotonics → TXA → tamponade → suture → UAE/hysterectomy
UAE requires stability; hysterectomy for exsanguinating decompensation
Coagulopathy + hypothermia + rising vasopressor need = surgical control now
rFVIIa is last-resort adjunct AFTER surgical control
Time-to-definitive-haemostasis is a mortality determinant
explanation.pearls: Massive transfusion protocol activation aims for 1:1:1 red cells:FFP:platelets with fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate 3-4 g when fibrinogen <2 g/L), calcium replacement, and active warming; permissive hypotension is a trauma concept and does not apply to peripartum haemorrhage where uteroplacental perfusion needs pressure.

options.rationale: Carboprost has already been given at appropriate intervals with failure; escalating to further doses in a decompensating patient causes bronchospasm and hypertension without meaningful additional haemostatic effect. Definitive intervention is required. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

Uterine artery embolisation is fertility-preserving and effective (85-95 percent success) but requires a haemodynamically stable patient who can tolerate the transfer and procedure. This patient is coagulopathic, hypothermic, requiring rising vasopressors, and bleeding ~200 mL every 5 minutes; transferring to the radiology suite risks decompensation in transit and delays definitive haemostasis. UAE is indicated for controlled ongoing bleeding in a stabilised patient, not for exsanguinating haemorrhage in theatre. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

rFVIIa is an off-label rescue therapy considered only after correction of pH, temperature, calcium and fibrinogen and after all surgical options have been exhausted. It is expensive, prothrombotic (thromboembolic events 5-10 percent), and does not substitute for definitive surgical control. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

Balloon tamponade is a single-device therapy; over-inflation risks uterine rupture and cervical injury. Sequential attempts at conservative measures that have already failed waste time in a decompensating patient. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)

In refractory PPH with ongoing haemorrhage, escalating vasopressor need, coagulopathy and hypothermia, the priority is definitive haemostasis over fertility preservation. Peripartum hysterectomy is the appropriate life-saving step when the patient is already in theatre, intubated, coagulopathic and continuing to bleed. Transfer to interventional radiology in an unstable coagulopathic patient with continuing 200 mL every 5 minutes bleeding introduces unacceptable risk. The RANZCOG PPH stepwise pathway explicitly places hysterectomy as the final surgical option and time-to-decision is a mortality determinant. Fertility conversations occurred antenatally but survival dominates in decompensated shock. (Source: RANZCOG PPH)
